metadata.specialty: Prehospital emergency care and traumatic brain injury
metadata.summary: This evidence-based guideline addresses prehospital assessment and management of suspected traumatic brain injury in adults and children, with an emphasis on preventing secondary brain injury. It covers physiological and neurological monitoring, airway and ventilation care, fluid resuscitation, and management of suspected increased intracranial pressure. It also addresses decisions about trauma-system destination and transport.

target_population: patients with suspected moderate to severe TBI

recognition: Continuous pulse oximetry can identify desaturation during intubation.

management.actions: Correct it immediately through appropriate airway positioning and continuous supplemental oxygen.

management.severity: Hypoxia persists despite increased supplemental oxygen flow and concentration
management.actions: Reassess oxygen saturation and respiratory effort after each step: reposition the airway while considering possible cervical spine injury; provide bag-valve-mask ventilation with suitable airway adjuncts; then use a supraglottic airway or have a trained professional perform endotracheal intubation.

prevention: Continuously monitor oxygen saturation in patients undergoing prehospital intubation and correct desaturation rapidly.
Minimize hypoxia around intubation through appropriate oxygenation and airway management.

toxicities.event: Inadvertent hyperventilation and hypocapnia during prehospital ventilation
toxicities.incidence: In a U.S. study, 15% of patients undergoing prehospital RSI had severe hyperventilation (pCO2<25) on hospital arrival, compared with 8% of non-intubated controls.
recognition: Capnography permits ongoing assessment, although its use alone does not guarantee that inadvertent hyperventilation will be prevented.

management.severity: Patients receiving positive pressure ventilation without signs of active cerebral herniation
management.actions: Use a normal breathing rate of approximately 10breaths per minute, monitor ETCO2, and avoid hyperventilation. The airway-treatment recommendation specifies ETCO2 35–45mmHg; the recommendation concerning suspected increased intracranial pressure specifies an eucapnia target of ETCO2 35–40.

management.severity: Signs of active and imminent cerebral herniation
management.actions: If hyperventilation is used, monitor by capnography and target ETCO2 30– 35.

prevention: Avoid hyperventilation in children and adults with TBI unless signs of active cerebral herniation are present.
Use ETCO2 monitoring and ventilatory aids, such as pressure-controlled bags, ventilation-rate timers, or ventilators, to support appropriate ventilation.

recognition: Monitor blood pressure frequently in intubated patients; the guideline identifies <100mmHg systolic blood pressure [SBP] as a threshold requiring attention in patients with suspected TBI.

management.actions: Administer intravenous fluids to treat hypotension and keep its duration as short as possible. Use isotonic fluids and/or blood products when indicated and available.

prevention: Monitor blood pressure frequently during prehospital care of intubated patients and seek to avoid hypotension around intubation.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Provide continuous supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula or face mask to patients with suspected severe TBI to reduce secondary injury from hypoxia.
Avoid prophylactic hyperventilation in children and adults with TBI when signs of active cerebral herniation are absent.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children and adults with TBI without signs of active cerebral herniation

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not administer mannitol or hypertonic saline to prophylactically treat suspected elevated ICP in the prehospital setting, whether or not signs of cerebral herniation are present.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with suspected elevated ICP, with or without signs of cerebral herniation

prophylaxis.recommendation: Prehospital TXA is not generally or widely indicated to prophylactically treat suspected ICH or elevated ICP; decisions may differ among health care systems, and additional evidence could support broader use.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with suspected ICH or elevated ICP

therapies_index.name: supplemental oxygen
therapies_index.mechanism: Increases oxygen delivery to address hypoxemia without raising the ventilation rate.
approved_indications: Prehospital care of patients with suspected severe TBI to prevent hypoxia.
Correction of hypoxemia identified during prehospital care.
therapies_index.administration: Provide continuously through a nasal cannula or face mask for suspected severe TBI; adjust delivery to maintain oxygen saturation above 90%.
monitoring: Continuously assess oxygen saturation with pulse oximetry.
Reassess oxygen saturation and respiratory effort after changes in airway or oxygen delivery.

therapies_index.name: airway re-positioning
approved_indications: Persistent signs of hypoxia despite increased supplemental oxygen.
therapies_index.administration: Reposition the airway while accounting for possible cervical spine injury; reassess oxygen saturation and respiratory effort afterward.

therapies_index.name: bag-valve-mask ventilation
approved_indications: Persistent hypoxia after supplemental oxygen and airway repositioning.
Inadequate oxygenation or ventilation requiring positive pressure support.
therapies_index.administration: Provide positive pressure breaths, using an appropriate airway adjunct when needed. For adults requiring ventilatory support, use approximately 10breaths per minute while targeting ETCO2 35–45mmHg.
key_toxicities: Excessive ventilation can produce hypocapnia, which is associated with worse outcomes after TBI.

therapies_index.name: oropharyngeal airway
approved_indications: Airway support during bag-valve-mask ventilation when hypoxia persists despite supplemental oxygen and airway repositioning.
therapies_index.administration: Use as an appropriately selected airway adjunct during bag-valve-mask ventilation.
monitoring: Reassess oxygen saturation and respiratory effort after its use.

therapies_index.name: supraglottic airway
approved_indications: Persistent hypoxia requiring escalation beyond supplemental oxygen and initial airway maneuvers.
therapies_index.administration: Placement is an airway option for a trained health care professional; reassess oxygen saturation and respiratory effort afterward.

therapies_index.name: esophageal tracheal airway
approved_indications: A supraglottic device considered when initial measures do not adequately correct oxygenation.

therapies_index.name: laryngeal mask airways
approved_indications: Supraglottic airway support considered when oxygenation remains inadequate after initial measures.

therapies_index.name: endotracheal intubation
approved_indications: Severe TBI with an inability to maintain an adequate airway.
Hypoxemia that supplemental oxygen does not correct.
Inadequate oxygenation or ventilation despite less invasive airway measures; patients with severe TBI and GCS <9 should be considered promptly for definitive advanced airway management.
therapies_index.administration: A trained health care professional performs the procedure. Confirm tracheal placement through bilateral breath sounds and ETCO2 detection and/or capnography.
monitoring: Continuously monitor oxygenation and ETCO2 after intubation.
Confirm tube placement by auscultation and ETCO2 detection and/or capnography.

therapies_index.name: RSI
approved_indications: A protocol that may facilitate prehospital endotracheal intubation.
therapies_index.administration: The document discusses medication-assisted intubation but does not specify a drug combination or dosing schedule.
key_toxicities: Studies cited by the guideline associated prehospital RSI with severe hypocarbia on hospital arrival.
Hypoxic episodes during prehospital intubation were associated with higher mortality in a cited study.
monitoring: Confirm tracheal tube placement using bilateral breath sounds and ETCO2 detection and/or capnography.
Continuously monitor oxygenation and ETCO2 and frequently measure blood pressure after intubation.

therapies_index.name: hyperventilation
therapies_index.mechanism: Lowering CO2 constricts cerebral microvasculature and reduces cerebral blood volume and ICP.
approved_indications: When addressing signs of active and imminent cerebral herniation, target ETCO2 of 30– 35 with capnography.
Avoid its prehospital use in children and adults with TBI when signs of active cerebral herniation are absent.
therapies_index.administration: If used for active and imminent herniation, adjust ventilation to ETCO2 of 30– 35; the discussion considers transient use when rapid surgical decompression or other intervention is unavailable.
key_toxicities: Cerebral vasoconstriction may further reduce blood flow and contribute to ischemia.
Routine or inadvertent hyperventilation is associated with worse outcomes after TBI.

therapies_index.name: intravenous fluids
therapies_index.mechanism: Volume replacement augments cardiac preload and supports cardiac output, blood pressure, and cerebral perfusion.
approved_indications: Treat prehospital hypotension or keep its duration as short as possible in patients with TBI.
therapies_index.administration: Administer intravenously; fluid selection and volume depend on the clinical circumstances.
key_toxicities: Resuscitation that causes hemodilution or secondary blood loss is a concern identified by the guideline.

therapies_index.name: isotonic fluids
therapies_index.mechanism: Intravascular volume replacement supports blood pressure and oxygen delivery.
approved_indications: Prehospital treatment of hypotension in patients with TBI, with blood products when indicated and available.
therapies_index.administration: Administer intravenously for hypotension; no specific isotonic-fluid dose is prescribed.

therapies_index.name: crystalloid fluids
therapies_index.mechanism: Increase cardiac preload to support cardiac output and peripheral oxygen delivery.
approved_indications: Volume resuscitation after trauma; in children, clinical evidence of reduced perfusion can warrant fluids despite an adequate blood pressure reading.
therapies_index.administration: The document describes a common prehospital approach of bolus infusion of 1 to 2 liters of crystalloid volume, without prescribing that amount for every patient.

therapies_index.name: normal saline
therapies_index.mechanism: As an isotonic solution, it produces little osmotic shift in theory; fluid replacement supports circulation.
approved_indications: Used as a comparison fluid for resuscitation in studies discussed by the guideline.
therapies_index.administration: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) may be delivered by intravenous bolus or infusion. A cited study compared 250ml of normal saline with other fluids.

therapies_index.name: Ringer’s lactate
approved_indications: Used as a comparator resuscitation fluid in studies discussed by the guideline.

therapies_index.name: lactated Ringer’s solution
approved_indications: Used as a comparison resuscitation fluid in a study of patients with TBI.

therapies_index.name: blood products
therapies_index.mechanism: Replenish intravascular volume to support cardiac function and oxygen delivery after hemorrhage.
approved_indications: Prehospital treatment of hypotension when indicated and available.
Timely treatment of hypotension in pediatric TBI was examined in a cited study.
therapies_index.administration: Use for resuscitation when indicated and available; the document provides no product-specific dose.

therapies_index.name: vasopressors
approved_indications: Included among treatments for pediatric hypotension examined by the cited PEGASUS study.

therapies_index.name: hypertonic saline
therapies_index.mechanism: Raises the osmotic gradient, drawing extracellular fluid into the vasculature and temporarily reducing ICP.
approved_indications: Hypertonic fluid resuscitation may be given prehospital to a patient with GCS <8 and suspected increased ICP.
The guideline advises against prophylactic prehospital hyperosmolar treatment of suspected elevated ICP, whether or not signs of cerebral herniation are present.
therapies_index.administration: Studied as a prehospital resuscitation fluid and as a bolus for ICP reduction in monitored hospital settings. The document lists clinically available hypertonic concentrations of 3%, 7.2%, 7.5%, 10%, and 23.4%, but establishes no optimal concentration or delivery method.
monitoring: ICP monitoring is described for studies of its use in operating-room or ICU settings.
A serum sodium target around 155–160mEq/L is described for hospital ICP management, but the guideline states that this target is not feasible prehospital.

therapies_index.name: hypertonic saline plus dextran
approved_indications: Evaluated as a resuscitation combination in cited trials; the guideline does not identify an additional benefit from dextran.
therapies_index.administration: A cited study compared 250ml of hypertonic saline plus dextran with other fluids.

therapies_index.name: dextran
approved_indications: Studied as an addition to hypertonic saline for resuscitation; cited research did not establish an added benefit.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated together with hypertonic saline; no separate dosing schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: hyperoncotic fluids
approved_indications: Discussed among fluid options used for trauma resuscitation, with inconsistent evidence of benefit in TBI.

therapies_index.name: hemoglobin substitutes
approved_indications: Discussed as resuscitation options studied after trauma; benefits for TBI treatment have been inconsistent.

therapies_index.name: mannitol
therapies_index.mechanism: As a hyperosmolar agent, increases the osmotic gradient and shifts extracellular fluid into the vasculature, temporarily lowering ICP.
approved_indications: Used to reduce ICP temporarily.
The guideline advises against prophylactic prehospital hyperosmolar treatment of suspected elevated ICP, with or without signs of cerebral herniation.

therapies_index.name: TXA
approved_indications: Studied prehospital as a possible means of limiting intracranial hemorrhage expansion; the guideline states that its prehospital use is not generally and widely indicated to prevent suspected ICH or elevated ICP.
therapies_index.administration: Prehospital initiation was evaluated in studies; no dose or administration schedule is specified.
key_toxicities: The cited BRAIN-PROTECT study reported increased mortality in its TXA-treated group.

therapies_index.name: sedative agents
approved_indications: Discussed as medication adjuncts for prehospital intubation.
therapies_index.administration: When feasible without delaying airway stabilization, measure GCS before administering these agents or after they have been metabolized.
monitoring: GCS assessment in relation to administration

therapies_index.name: paralytic agents
approved_indications: Discussed as medication adjuncts for intubation.
therapies_index.administration: When feasible without delaying airway stabilization, measure GCS before administration or after the drugs have been metabolized.
monitoring: GCS assessment in relation to administration

therapies_index.name: surgical decompression
approved_indications: Discussed as a definitive intervention that may be needed for cerebral herniation or an intracranial mass lesion.

therapies_index.name: craniotomy
approved_indications: Listed among neurosurgical interventions assessed as study outcomes.

therapies_index.name: ventriculostomy
approved_indications: Listed among neurosurgical interventions assessed as study outcomes.

conditions.name: traumatic brain injury (TBI)
conditions.description: A direct or indirect force affecting the brain disrupts normal brain function. Injury ranges from concussion to coma or death. After the initial injury, cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemia, increased intracranial pressure (ICP), metabolic disturbances, hypoxia, and temperature instability can cause secondary injury.
conditions.epidemiology: Worldwide, 69 million people sustain TBI annually. Its incidence in low- and middle-income countries is three times that in high-income countries. Reported fatality rates range from 5.2/100,000/year in France to 80.73/100,000/year in South Africa. Most TBIs are mild. In the United States, TBI accounts for 2.87 million emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and deaths annually; approximately one-third of these events occur in children. The fatality rate from all causes of TBI is 22% higher in rural than urban areas of the United States.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Manifestations range from preserved consciousness to coma. Following physical trauma, GCS <15, loss of consciousness, multisystem trauma requiring an advanced airway, or a reported post-traumatic seizure increases concern for moderate-severe TBI. Hypoxia, abnormal blood pressure, altered ventilation or temperature, and pupillary abnormalities may accompany the injury.

subtypes.name: mild TBI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes concussions and accounts for the majority of TBIs; distinguishing it from more serious injury may not be immediately possible before hospital arrival.

subtypes.name: moderate to severe TBI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May require advanced airway management and places patients at risk of secondary insults from hypoxia, hypotension, and abnormal ventilation.

subtypes.name: severe TBI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May involve coma or death; deterioration and death can occur within the first few hours after injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess consciousness and repeatedly document neurologic status to inform injury assessment, prognosis, and allocation of trauma resources.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After assessment and stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation; reassess every 30minutes and after a change in mental status.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Combines eye-opening, verbal, and motor responses. Seizures, the post-ictal phase, ingestions, overdose, administered medications, hypoxia, and hypotension can affect the score. A worsening score can signal neurologic deterioration.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess consciousness using developmentally appropriate verbal and motor responses.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For pre-verbal children; the standard GCS protocol applies to children over 2 years of age.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The modified verbal response accommodates preverbal behavior.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess neurologic changes and contribute to diagnosis and prognosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After resuscitation and stabilization; document findings and communicate them to the receiving facility.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assess size, symmetry, response to light, ocular or orbital injury, and examination confounders. Asymmetry >1mm is clinically significant; a fixed pupil has <1mm response to bright light. A single finding of asymmetry neither reliably identifies nor localizes an intracranial mass lesion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify hypoxemia and monitor oxygenation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Continuously during prehospital care of suspected TBI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Arterial hemoglobin saturation <90% indicates hypoxemia in the assessment recommendations.

diagnostic_workup.test: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurement
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect and track hypotension or hypertension that may contribute to secondary injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Frequently during prehospital care, every 5–10min, or continuously if possible.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The assessment recommendations flag <100mmHg systolic blood pressure [SBP] and 150mmHg SBP or higher for monitoring. Recommended targets depend on age and other factors; no definitive adult cutoff is established.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess ventilation and detect hypo- or hyperventilation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Continuously for patients with an altered level of consciousness and for intubated patients.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The assessment recommendations specify end tidal CO2 between 35 and 45mmHg and identify values less than 35 as hyperventilation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify hypo- or hyperthermia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During prehospital assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline describes euthermia as 98–99degrees Fahrenheit/36–37degrees Celsius.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate intracranial injury at a receiving facility with appropriate imaging capability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Access to promptly available CT is a destination consideration for suspected moderate-severe TBI.

staging.additional_rules: The guideline refers to mild, moderate, and severe injury but does not set out a complete severity-staging system. It states that GCS 12–15 reflects higher integrative brain function.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The motor component provides prognostic information similar to the full score. Serial scores, including changes between the scene and hospital, inform prognosis, although studies differed on whether the hospital score better predicts function.

prognostic_tools.name: Pediatric GCS (P-GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Adapts assessment to preverbal children; a cited prospective cohort found comparable accuracy for identifying clinically important TBI below age 2years.

prognostic_tools.name: simplified motor score (SMS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Studies found prognostic accuracy similar to the complete GCS or its motor component in several settings, without establishing superior accuracy across studies.

prognostic_tools.name: simplified verbal score (SVS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Examined as an alternative to the complete GCS; the guideline does not establish superior prognostic accuracy.

prognostic_tools.name: revised trauma score (RTS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Studies cited by the guideline found that scores incorporating GCS predicted outcomes; one analysis identified in-hospital RTS among its best predictors.

prognostic_tools.name: trauma and injury severity score (TRISS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: In cited studies, this score predicted outcomes, including survival to hospital discharge.

prognostic_tools.name: National Early Warning Score (NEWS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: In one cited prospective cohort, prehospital NEWS was among the best predictors of short term 24-hour mortality.

prognostic_tools.name: Corticosteroid Randomization after Significant Head Injury (CRASH) prognosis calculator
prognostic_tools.interpretation: A cited study used it to predict favorable GOS at 6months and mortality at 14days in patients presenting with GCS 3.

conditions.name: moderate to severe TBI
conditions.description: A more serious range of traumatic brain injury in which prevention of secondary insults and access to definitive neurotrauma care are central concerns during prehospital management.
conditions.clinical_presentation: In a patient who has sustained physical trauma, GCS <15, loss of consciousness, multisystem trauma requiring an advanced airway, or a reported post-traumatic seizure raises the likelihood of moderate-severe injury. Patients may develop hypoxemia, hypotension, altered consciousness, or pupillary abnormalities.

subtypes.name: severe TBI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May involve marked impairment of consciousness and require advanced airway management.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess neurologic status and its change over time.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After initial airway, breathing, and circulation assessment and stabilization; reassess every 30minutes and with a change in mental status.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The score may change after prehospital stabilization. Combining it with pupillary findings can improve prognostic accuracy, but an unfavorable combination does not invariably predict a poor outcome.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify changes relevant to neurologic deterioration and prognosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After resuscitation and stabilization.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: New asymmetry or reduced reactivity can suggest worsening intracranial pathology, although pupillary findings alone are not specific for its anatomy or severity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect hypoxemia, including during airway management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Continuously in prehospital care.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Oxygen saturation <90% identifies hypoxemia; lower values are associated with worse outcomes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize blood pressure abnormalities and guide prompt response.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Repeatedly during prehospital care.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Prehospital hypotension is associated with poorer outcomes. Cited studies question whether a single SBP threshold adequately describes this risk.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor ventilation and identify hyperventilation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For patients with altered consciousness or receiving ventilatory support.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The ventilation recommendations target ETCO2 35–45mmHg during routine respiratory support.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate intracranial injury at the receiving facility.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The guideline recommends direct transport of suspected moderate-severe TBI to a facility with immediately available CT, prompt neurosurgical care, and capacity to monitor ICP and treat intracranial hypertension.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Scores and their changes inform prognosis and destination decisions. The motor response is particularly informative, while pupillary findings add prognostic information.

prognostic_tools.name: simplified motor score (SMS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: May provide diagnostic and prognostic utility similar to the full GCS in adults within trauma systems that use it.

conditions.name: severe TBI
conditions.description: A serious form of traumatic brain injury associated with substantial morbidity and mortality; death often occurs within the first few hours after injury.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May present with profoundly depressed consciousness, coma, impaired airway protection, abnormal pupils, or signs concerning for increased ICP. The guideline discusses GCS <9 in relation to consideration of advanced airway management and to signs of possible herniation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Track consciousness and detect deterioration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation, and before sedative or paralytic agents when possible without delaying airway stabilization.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: GCS <9 is identified among signs of possible increased ICP or herniation and in discussion of advanced airway management. Even GCS 3 does not invariably imply an unfavorable functional outcome.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible deterioration and contribute to prognosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After resuscitation and stabilization.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Fixed, dilated, or asymmetric pupils can suggest serious intracranial pathology but do not invariably predict an adverse functional outcome.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect and permit rapid correction of hypoxemia, particularly around intubation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Throughout prehospital care.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline identifies SpO2< 90% as hypoxemia in its airway recommendations.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify hypotension and hypertension associated with adverse outcomes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Frequently during prehospital care and in intubated patients.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In pediatric isolated severe TBI, a cited retrospective study associated admission SBP <75th percentile with increased in-hospital mortality across age subgroups.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor ventilation and detect inadvertent hyperventilation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Continuously in intubated patients.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline associates hyperventilation with poorer outcomes and recommends monitoring ETCO2.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify intracranial injury at a capable receiving facility.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As part of definitive evaluation after transport for suspected moderate-severe TBI.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)

risk_groups.criteria: Presentation with GCS 3 together with bilateral fixed pupils.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: In a cited study, favorable GOS occurred in 6.9% of patients with this combination; it was not invariably associated with a poor outcome.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: The motor response and pupillary examination together improve prognostic assessment, but neither alone justifies assuming that recovery is impossible.

prognostic_tools.name: Corticosteroid Randomization after Significant Head Injury (CRASH) prognosis calculator
prognostic_tools.interpretation: In a cited study of patients presenting with GCS 3, it accurately predicted favorable GOS at 6months; observed mortality at 14days was 66%, below the calculator's predicted 81%.

prognostic_tools.name: Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) IV
prognostic_tools.interpretation: In a cited study of patients presenting with GCS 3, those with favorable GOS had lower scores.

conditions.name: suspected increased ICP
conditions.description: A potential secondary complication of TBI. Expanding intracranial mass lesions and cerebral edema are described as common causes; worsening pressure can lead to herniation.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible indicators include Cushing’s triad—hypertension, bradycardia, and an irregular breathing pattern—GCS <9, posturing, lateralizing findings, progressive neurologic deterioration, and unilateral or bilateral fixed, dilated pupils. These clinical signs may lack sufficient sensitivity or predictive value.

subtypes.name: active cerebral herniation
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May be suspected from neurologic deterioration, posturing or lateralizing findings, and abnormal pupillary findings; the guideline also lists Cushing’s triad and GCS <9 among concerning signs.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize depressed consciousness or progressive neurologic deterioration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During serial prehospital neurologic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: GCS <9 is listed among classic indicators. A decrease of more than two points from the patient's prior best score is described as a possible sign of cerebral herniation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify new abnormalities that may signal increased ICP or herniation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After resuscitation and stabilization, with reassessment when neurologic status changes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: New anisocoria greater than 1mm, reduced light response, or fixed, dilated pupils may be concerning. A single asymmetry measurement is neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific to identify or localize an intracranial mass lesion.

diagnostic_workup.test: Blood pressure, heart rate, and breathing pattern assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize the features of Cushing’s triad.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During assessment for suspected increased ICP or active herniation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The triad comprises hypertension, bradycardia, and an irregular breathing pattern; its presence is concerning but clinical indicators may not be sufficiently sensitive.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor ETCO2 when managing ventilation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During prehospital ventilatory management, including when hyperventilation is used for signs of active and imminent herniation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The recommendations target ETCO2 of 35–40 for eucapnia and ETCO2 of 30– 35 when hyperventilation is used for active and imminent herniation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate intracranial lesions at a receiving facility.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Access to immediate CT is specified for the destination of patients with suspected moderate-severe TBI.

prognostic_tools.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Serial decline contributes to recognition of possible herniation, but clinical signs alone have limited predictive value.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with suspected TBI receiving prehospital care.
decision_rules: Monitor for and promptly address hypoxemia (<90% arterial hemoglobin saturation), hypotension (<100mmHg systolic blood pressure [SBP]), hypertension (150mmHg SBP or higher), hyperventilation (end tidal CO2 less than 35), and hypo- or hyperthermia.
Measure systolic and diastolic blood pressure by the most accurate available method every 5–10min, or monitor it continuously when feasible.

recommended_regimens.name: Continuous pulse oximetry and supplemental oxygen
recommended_regimens.summary: Measure oxygen saturation continuously and give supplemental oxygen to keep it above 90%.

recommended_regimens.name: Blood pressure monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: Measure systolic and diastolic blood pressure repeatedly or continuously when possible.

recommended_regimens.name: Temperature assessment and maintenance of euthermia
recommended_regimens.summary: Measure temperature before hospital arrival and take steps to maintain euthermia at 98–99degrees Fahrenheit/36–37degrees Celsius.

response_assessment.method: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurement
response_assessment.interpretation: Identify blood pressure abnormalities early enough to address them promptly.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Prehospital services without resource limitations should make appropriately sized oxygenation, blood pressure, and temperature equipment available for routine use in adults and children by trained personnel.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with TBI receiving prehospital care.
decision_rules: Aim for an age-specific SBP at or above the 75th percentile; the stated targets are 28days and younger >70mmHg, 1–12months > 84mmHg, 1–5years >90mmHg, and 6years and older > 100mmHg.
Use appropriately sized pediatric oximetry sensors and blood pressure cuffs.
If pediatric blood pressure cuffs are unavailable in a resource-limited setting, continuously assess mental status, peripheral pulse quality, and capillary refill time as surrogate measures.

recommended_regimens.name: Age-specific systolic blood pressure targeting
recommended_regimens.summary: Target pediatric SBP to the 75th percentile or higher for age following TBI.

recommended_regimens.name: Pediatric oxygenation and blood pressure monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: Use pediatric-sized oximetry sensors and appropriately sized cuffs when measuring oxygenation and blood pressure.

alternative_regimens.name: Continuous assessment of mental status, peripheral pulses, and capillary refill time
alternative_regimens.summary: Use these findings as surrogate blood pressure measures.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Resource-limited settings in which pediatric blood pressure cuffs are unavailable.

response_assessment.timepoint: Continuously when pediatric blood pressure cuffs are unavailable
response_assessment.method: Mental status, peripheral pulse quality, and capillary refill time
response_assessment.interpretation: Use as surrogate measures rather than assigning an unmeasured blood pressure.

supportive_care: In children, clinical evidence of reduced perfusion can warrant fluid resuscitation even when the recorded blood pressure is adequate.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document specifies cuff sizes of Infants: 6x12cm; Children: 9x18cm; Small adult: 12x22cm; Adult: 16x30cm; and Large adult: 16x36cm.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with TBI receiving prehospital care.
decision_rules: Aim for SBP of 110mmHg or greater after TBI; lower readings are associated with worse outcomes, and an optimal target may be higher.
Aim for oxygen saturation of 90% or greater; an optimal target may be higher.

recommended_regimens.name: Adult systolic blood pressure targeting
recommended_regimens.summary: Target SBP to 110mmHg or greater without treating that value as a proven hard cutoff.

recommended_regimens.name: Oxygen saturation targeting
recommended_regimens.summary: Target oxygen saturation to 90% or greater without treating that value as a proven hard cutoff.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that optimal values depend on multiple factors and that specific hard cutoff values have not been established.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with suspected severe TBI receiving prehospital care.
decision_rules: Provide continuous oxygen supplementation to reduce secondary injury associated with hypoxia.
If SpO2< 90% is detected, immediately check airway positioning and provide continuous supplemental oxygen.

recommended_regimens.name: Continuous supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula or face mask
recommended_regimens.summary: Give continuous supplemental oxygen before hospital arrival to patients with suspected severe TBI.

recommended_regimens.name: Continuous pulse oximetry and immediate correction of hypoxemia
recommended_regimens.summary: Continuously monitor oxygenation and promptly correct SpO2< 90% through appropriate airway positioning and supplemental oxygen.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The treatment discussion also emphasizes preventing hypoxia before oxygen saturation falls.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with suspected TBI whose central cyanosis or pulse-oximetry hypoxemia persists despite increased flow and concentration of supplemental oxygen.
decision_rules: First reposition the airway while accounting for possible cervical spine injury.
If hypoxia continues, provide positive pressure ventilation with bag-valve-mask ventilation and suitable airway adjuncts.
If oxygenation or ventilation remains inadequate, use a supraglottic airway or have a trained professional perform endotracheal intubation.
Recheck oxygen saturation and respiratory effort after each escalation.

recommended_regimens.name: Stepwise airway repositioning and bag-valve-mask ventilation
recommended_regimens.summary: Escalate from airway repositioning to positive pressure ventilation with suitable adjuncts when hypoxia persists despite supplemental oxygen.

alternative_regimens.name: Supraglottic airway or endotracheal intubation
alternative_regimens.summary: A trained health care professional may establish an advanced airway when earlier measures do not adequately correct oxygenation or ventilation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent hypoxia or inadequate ventilation after supplemental oxygen and earlier airway measures.

response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent impairment determines whether to proceed to the next airway measure.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Airway repositioning must take possible cervical spine injury into account.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with signs of severe TBI who cannot maintain an adequate airway or whose hypoxemia is not corrected with supplemental oxygen.
decision_rules: Establish an airway by the most appropriate available means.
Immediately consider definitive advanced airway management when severe TBI is accompanied by depressed mental status (GCS <9).
When endotracheal intubation is used, confirm tracheal placement through bilateral breath sounds and ETCO2 detection and/or capnography.

recommended_regimens.name: Airway establishment
recommended_regimens.summary: Use the most appropriate available airway method when severe TBI is accompanied by inadequate airway maintenance or hypoxemia uncorrected by oxygen.

recommended_regimens.name: Endotracheal tube placement confirmation and physiologic monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: For systems using endotracheal intubation, including RSI, verify tube placement by bilateral breath sounds and ETCO2 detection and/or capnography; continuously monitor oxygenation and ETCO2 and measure blood pressure frequently.

response_assessment.method: Bilateral breath sounds on auscultation and ETCO2 detection and/or capnography
response_assessment.interpretation: Use these findings to confirm placement in the trachea.

response_assessment.method: Oxygenation and ETCO2 monitoring, with frequent blood pressure measurement
response_assessment.interpretation: Detect physiologic abnormalities requiring prompt correction.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline emphasizes trained personnel, maintained intubation skills, and avoidance of hypoxia, hypotension, and hyperventilation around intubation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients requiring positive pressure ventilation, without signs of active cerebral herniation.
decision_rules: Ventilate at a normal breathing rate, approximately 10breaths per minute, while monitoring ETCO2.
Target eucapnia and avoid hyperventilation and hypocapnia.
Use ventilation aids to support appropriate rates and reduce both excessive and inadequate ventilation.

recommended_regimens.name: Normoventilation with capnography
recommended_regimens.summary: For positive pressure ventilation, use approximately 10breaths per minute with ETCO2 35–45mmHg. The recommendation addressing avoidance of hypocapnia also specifies an eucapnia target of ETCO2 of 35–40.

recommended_regimens.name: Ventilatory adjuncts
recommended_regimens.summary: Use aids such as pressure-controlled bags, ventilation-rate timers, ETCO2 monitoring, or ventilators to support appropriate ventilation.

not_recommended.name: Routine hyperventilation without signs of active cerebral herniation
not_recommended.reason: The guideline strongly advises against it because hyperventilation can reduce cerebral blood flow and is associated with worse outcomes.

response_assessment.interpretation: Avoid ETCO2 <35mmHg; assess ventilation against the stated eucapnia targets.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In patients with altered consciousness, the assessment recommendations call for continuous capnography to maintain end tidal CO2 between 35 and 45mmHg.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adults with TBI and signs of active and imminent cerebral herniation.
decision_rules: Assess for signs including Cushing’s triad, GCS <9, posturing or lateralizing findings, progressive neurologic deterioration, and unilateral or bilateral fixed, dilated pupil(s).
If hyperventilation is used for active and imminent herniation, monitor it by capnography and target ETCO2 of 30– 35.
Do not give mannitol or hypertonic saline prophylactically for suspected elevated ICP, whether or not signs of herniation are present.

recommended_regimens.name: Capnography-guided hyperventilation for active and imminent herniation
recommended_regimens.summary: When hyperventilation is used to address active and imminent herniation, target ETCO2 of 30– 35 and monitor with capnography.

not_recommended.name: Prophylactic mannitol or hypertonic saline for suspected elevated ICP
not_recommended.reason: The guideline weakly advises against prophylactic prehospital use because studies have not demonstrated improved outcomes from prehospital hyperosmolar fluids for this purpose.

response_assessment.timepoint: During hyperventilation used for active and imminent herniation

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline describes uncertainty about the balance of risks and benefits of hyperventilation in this subgroup. The treatment discussion says transient use may be considered when surgical decompression or other interventions will not be rapidly available; it also notes that clinical signs of herniation have moderate to low predictive values.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with TBI and prehospital hypotension.
decision_rules: Give intravenous fluids to treat hypotension and keep its duration as short as possible.
Use isotonic fluids and/or blood products when indicated and available.
Tailor resuscitation to the clinical circumstances, particularly when hypotension occurs with polytrauma rather than isolated TBI.

recommended_regimens.name: Intravenous fluid resuscitation
recommended_regimens.summary: Administer intravenous fluids before hospital arrival to treat hypotension or minimize the time spent hypotensive.

recommended_regimens.name: Isotonic fluids and/or blood products
recommended_regimens.summary: Resuscitate hypotensive patients with isotonic fluids and/or blood products when blood products are indicated and available.

response_assessment.interpretation: Identify and address persistent hypotension while limiting its duration.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline notes that evidence does not establish an outcome advantage for any one prehospital fluid type. Resuscitation seeks to restore perfusion without causing hemodilution or secondary blood loss.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with GCS scores <8 and suspected increased ICP in the prehospital setting.
decision_rules: Hypertonic fluid resuscitation may be given in this specified circumstance.
Distinguish this option from prophylactic hyperosmolar treatment of suspected elevated ICP, which the guideline advises against.

alternative_regimens.name: Hypertonic fluid resuscitation
alternative_regimens.summary: Hypertonic fluid resuscitation may be administered when GCS is <8 and increased ICP is suspected; the recommendation is graded Weak.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: GCS scores <8 with suspected increased ICP.

not_recommended.name: Prophylactic hyperosmolar therapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against prophylactic prehospital treatment of suspected elevated ICP, with or without herniation signs, because an improvement in outcomes has not been demonstrated for this use.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The permission for hypertonic fluid resuscitation is a Weak recommendation in the fluid-resuscitation section; the separate recommendation against prophylactic hyperosmolar therapy is also Weak.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with TBI for whom prehospital prophylaxis of suspected ICH or elevated ICP is being considered.
decision_rules: Do not treat prehospital TXA as a generally or widely indicated prophylactic intervention for suspected ICH or elevated ICP.
The guideline allows that health care systems may reach different decisions and that further evidence could support broader use.

not_recommended.name: Routine prehospital TXA for prophylaxis of suspected ICH or elevated ICP
not_recommended.reason: The guideline states that this use is not generally or widely indicated. It describes uncertain benefit in severe TBI and differing findings across cited studies.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation is graded Strong but does not rule out differing health-system decisions or future changes as evidence develops.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with suspected moderate-severe TBI requiring a prehospital destination decision.
decision_rules: Arrange direct transport to a facility with immediately available CT neuroimaging, prompt neurosurgical care, and the ability to monitor ICP and treat intracranial hypertension.
Choose the transport mode that minimizes the interval until needed definitive intervention.
When direct transport to a trauma center is not possible, stabilization at a non-trauma center followed by transfer within an established trauma system may occur.

recommended_regimens.name: Direct transport to a neurotrauma-capable facility
recommended_regimens.summary: Transport patients with suspected moderate-severe TBI directly to a facility offering immediate CT, timely neurosurgical care, ICP monitoring, and treatment of intracranial hypertension.

recommended_regimens.name: Transport mode selected for timely definitive intervention
recommended_regimens.summary: Select ground or air transport according to which approach minimizes the interval to the interventions the patient needs.

alternative_regimens.name: Stabilization at a non-trauma center followed by transfer
alternative_regimens.summary: Initial stabilization outside a trauma center with subsequent transfer may occur within an established trauma system; this recommendation is graded Weak.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Direct transport to a trauma center is not possible.

supportive_care: Address immediate threats to life and prevent secondary injury while determining the receiving facility.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline calls for organized regional trauma systems and EMS destination protocols. It reports that evidence has not established a definitive outcome advantage for direct versus indirect trauma-center transport in adults with TBI, or for direct transport to LevelI rather than LevelII trauma centers.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pediatric patients with suspected TBI, including those with severe TBI in metropolitan areas.
decision_rules: Prefer a pediatric trauma center or an adult trauma center with additional qualifications for treating children over a LevelI or II adult trauma center without those qualifications.
In a metropolitan area, transport children with severe TBI directly to a pediatric trauma center when one is available.

recommended_regimens.name: Transport to a pediatric-capable trauma center
recommended_regimens.summary: For suspected pediatric TBI, prefer a pediatric trauma center or an adult trauma center qualified to treat children.

recommended_regimens.name: Direct pediatric trauma-center transport
recommended_regimens.summary: In metropolitan areas, directly transport children with severe TBI to an available pediatric trauma center.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline notes that evidence for adolescents does not definitively establish an advantage of pediatric over adult trauma centers. Transport-mode decisions must still account for time to specialist intervention.

special_populations.considerations: Hypotension and hypoxemia also worsen outcomes in children with severe TBI, although high-quality pediatric evidence on prehospital physiological monitoring is limited. The guideline advises targeting systolic blood pressure at the 75th percentile for age or higher: 28days and younger >70mmHg; 1–12months > 84mmHg; 1–5years >90mmHg; 6years and older > 100mmHg. Blood pressure and oxygenation assessments require equipment sized for children.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use pediatric-sized oximetry sensors and blood pressure cuffs. Give fluids when clinical signs indicate reduced perfusion, even if the blood pressure reading is adequate. The recommendation against routine prehospital hyperventilation also applies to children, but its long-term effects in pediatric TBI have not been studied; that recommendation relies on indirect adult evidence. Prefer a pediatric trauma center or an adult trauma center qualified to treat children over an adult LevelI or II center without pediatric qualifications. In metropolitan areas, transport children with severe TBI directly to a pediatric trauma center when one is available.

special_populations.considerations: Developmental immaturity makes the standard GCS unsuitable for infants and preverbal children because expected verbal and motor responses differ from those of older patients.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use P-GCS for preverbal children; follow the standard adult GCS protocol for children over 2 years of age.

special_populations.considerations: At the same GCS level, older patients may have more severe injuries than younger patients. The guideline notes that age may affect the optimal blood pressure threshold after TBI, but the evidence cited for age-specific thresholds comes from observational studies. Retrospective evidence suggests that triage based on GCS may need to account for age.
Pediatric blood pressure cuffs may be unavailable.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: When pediatric cuffs are unavailable, continuously monitor and document mental status, peripheral pulse quality, and capillary refill time as surrogate measures.

recommendations.statement: Closely monitor patients with suspected TBI before hospital arrival for hypoxemia (<90% arterial hemoglobin saturation), hypotension (<100mmHg systolic blood pressure [SBP]), hypertension (150mmHg SBP or higher), hyperventilation (end tidal CO2 less than 35), and hypo- or hyperthermia.
recommendations.rationale: Even brief hypoxia or hypotension can harm the injured brain, particularly when both occur together.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: For children after TBI, aim for an SBP at or above the 75th percentile for age. The stated targets are: 28days and younger >70mmHg; 1–12months > 84mmHg; 1–5years >90mmHg; and 6years and older > 100mmHg.
recommendations.rationale: Pediatric studies associate SBP below the 75th percentile with poorer outcomes.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: For adults after TBI, target an SBP of 110mmHg or greater; an optimal target may be higher. No firm cutoff has been established, and the best target depends on multiple factors.
recommendations.rationale: Lower SBP values are associated with worse outcomes.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Measure blood oxygen saturation continuously with pulse oximetry during prehospital care and give supplemental oxygen to keep saturation above 90%.
recommendations.rationale: Monitoring and addressing oxygenation can help prevent hypoxic secondary injury.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Use pediatric pulse-oximetry sensors of an appropriate size for children.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: After TBI, target oxygen saturation of 90% or greater; an optimal target may be higher. No firm cutoff is established, and the best level depends on multiple factors.
recommendations.rationale: Saturation below this level is associated with worse outcomes.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Measure systolic and diastolic blood pressure before hospital arrival using the most accurate available method, repeating measurements every 5–10min or monitoring continuously when feasible.
recommendations.rationale: Frequent measurements help identify and promptly address blood pressure abnormalities.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Measure children's blood pressure with appropriately sized pediatric cuffs. Where such cuffs are unavailable because of limited resources, continuously monitor and document mental status, peripheral pulse quality, and capillary refill time as substitutes.
recommendations.context: Pediatric assessment in settings with or without pediatric blood pressure cuffs.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Match blood pressure cuff size to the patient: Infants, 6x12cm; Children, 9x18cm; Small adult, 12x22cm; Adult, 16x30cm; and Large adult, 16x36cm.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: For every patient with altered consciousness, assess ventilation before hospital arrival using continuous capnography and maintain end tidal CO2 between 35 and 45mmHg.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Measure temperature before hospital arrival and take steps to maintain euthermia at 98–99degrees Fahrenheit/36–37degrees Celsius.
recommendations.rationale: The reviewed temperature study associated euthermia with better outcomes.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Outside resource-limited settings, keep appropriately sized oxygenation, blood pressure, and temperature measuring equipment available for routine use by trained prehospital professionals caring for children and adults.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Use the standard adult GCS assessment protocol for children over 2 years of age and the P-GCS for pre-verbal children.
recommendations.rationale: The standard GCS does not account adequately for the expected responses of preverbal children.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale and Other Assessment Scales

recommendations.statement: Report the GCS score every 30minutes before hospital arrival and whenever mental status changes. Document factors that may confound the score, including seizures and the post-ictal phase, ingestions and drug overdose, and prehospital medications that affect GCS.
recommendations.rationale: Repeated scores can reveal improvement or deterioration over time.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale and Other Assessment Scales

recommendations.statement: Obtain the GCS through direct interaction with the patient: give verbal instructions or, if the patient cannot follow commands, apply a painful stimulus such as nail bed pressure or an axillary pinch.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale and Other Assessment Scales

recommendations.statement: Measure GCS after evaluating airway, breathing, and circulation, establishing a clear airway, and completing any necessary ventilatory or circulatory resuscitation.
recommendations.rationale: Hypoxia and hypotension can impair neurologic responses and require immediate treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale and Other Assessment Scales

recommendations.statement: When feasible without delaying airway stabilization, measure GCS before giving sedative or paralytic agents; otherwise, assess it after those drugs have been metabolized.
recommendations.context: GCS assessment around sedation or paralysis.
recommendations.rationale: These agents may prevent accurate scoring.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale and Other Assessment Scales

recommendations.statement: Have prehospital professionals trained to administer GCS in both adults and children perform the assessment.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale and Other Assessment Scales

recommendations.statement: Communicate the prehospital GCS score and any changes in it to the receiving facility during every communication and on arrival.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale and Other Assessment Scales

recommendations.statement: In trauma systems organized to use these measures, the SMS or the GCS motor component alone may be used for prehospital neurologic assessment in adults; they may offer diagnostic and prognostic utility similar to the complete GCS.
recommendations.rationale: Reviewed studies found broadly similar predictive accuracy, although no alternative was consistently superior to complete GCS.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale and Other Assessment Scales

recommendations.statement: Examine the pupils after prehospital resuscitation and stabilization; record the findings and communicate them to the receiving facility to inform diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis.
recommendations.rationale: Pupillary findings can inform immediate decisions and prognosis, but disturbances during resuscitation can affect the examination.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Pupil Examination

recommendations.statement: During pupillary assessment, examine and document orbital or ocular trauma; compare the left and right pupils, with clinically significant diameter asymmetry defined as >1mm; note unilateral or bilateral dilation and fixed, dilated pupils, with a fixed pupil defined by <1mm response to bright light; and record factors that may confound the examination.
recommendations.context: Required components of the pupillary examination.
recommendations.rationale: Traumatic and nontraumatic factors can alter pupillary findings.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment: Pupil Examination

recommendations.statement: Give every patient with suspected severe TBI continuous supplemental oxygen through a nasal cannula or face mask before hospital arrival.
recommendations.rationale: The aim is to reduce secondary insults caused by hypoxia.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Airway, Oxygenation, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Use continuous pulse oximetry to detect hypoxemia (oxygen saturation [SpO2]< 90%) and correct it immediately by positioning the airway appropriately and providing continuous supplemental oxygen.
recommendations.context: Recognition and immediate treatment of hypoxemia.
recommendations.rationale: Hypoxemia is a strong predictor of outcome after acute TBI.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Airway, Oxygenation, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: If central cyanosis or pulse-oximetry hypoxemia persists despite increasing continuous supplemental oxygen flow and concentration, proceed stepwise: reposition the airway while considering possible cervical spine injury; provide positive-pressure ventilation, such as bag-valve-mask ventilation, with appropriate airway adjuncts; and/or use a supraglottic airway or have a trained professional perform endotracheal intubation. Reassess oxygen saturation and respiratory effort after each step.
recommendations.context: Escalation when supplemental oxygen does not resolve hypoxia.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Airway, Oxygenation, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Establish an airway by the most suitable available method when a patient has signs of severe TBI and cannot maintain an adequate airway, or when supplemental oxygen does not correct hypoxemia.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Airway, Oxygenation, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: EMS systems using endotracheal intubation protocols, including RSI, should verify tracheal tube placement through bilateral breath sounds on auscultation and ETCO2 detection and/or capnography. For intubated prehospital patients, continuously monitor oxygenation and ETCO2 and measure blood pressure frequently.
recommendations.context: Verification and monitoring after prehospital intubation.
recommendations.rationale: Monitoring helps identify ventilation or oxygenation problems and other secondary insults.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Airway, Oxygenation, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: For patients receiving positive-pressure respiratory support, use normal breathing rates of approximately 10breaths per minute with ETCO2 35–45mmHg, and avoid hyperventilation (ETCO2 <35mmHg). Use aids such as pressure-controlled bags, ventilation-rate timers, ETCO2 monitoring, and ventilators to support appropriate ventilation and avoid both inadequate and excessive ventilation.
recommendations.rationale: These measures seek to limit secondary insults associated with abnormal ventilation.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Airway, Oxygenation, and Ventilation

recommendations.statement: Administer intravenous fluids before hospital arrival to treat hypotension and/or keep its duration as short as possible.
recommendations.rationale: Restoring perfusion can help prevent secondary brain injury associated with hypotension.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Fluid Resuscitation

recommendations.statement: Treat hypotensive patients before hospital arrival with isotonic fluids and/or blood products when indicated and available.
recommendations.context: Choice of resuscitation fluid for hypotension.
recommendations.rationale: Volume repletion is intended to restore blood pressure and oxygen delivery.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Fluid Resuscitation

recommendations.statement: Hypertonic fluid resuscitation may be given before hospital arrival to patients with GCS scores <8 when increased ICP is suspected.
recommendations.context: Possible use of hypertonic fluid resuscitation.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence comparing resuscitation fluids shows limited and uncertain differences in patient outcomes.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Fluid Resuscitation

recommendations.statement: Avoid hyperventilation during prehospital care of children and adults with TBI unless there are signs of active cerebral herniation. Such signs include Cushing’s triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing pattern), GCS <9, posturing or lateralizing findings, progressive neurologic deterioration, and unilateral or bilateral fixed, dilated pupil(s).
recommendations.context: Ventilation when active cerebral herniation is not evident.
recommendations.rationale: Routine hyperventilation is associated with worse outcomes in TBI.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Hyperventilation and Hyperosmolar Therapy for Suspected Increased Intracranial Pressure

recommendations.statement: Use capnography to monitor ventilation, aim for eucapnia with ETCO2 of 35–40, and avoid hypocapnia.
recommendations.context: Ventilation target in prehospital TBI care.
recommendations.rationale: Hypocapnia associated with hyperventilation may reduce cerebral blood flow.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Hyperventilation and Hyperosmolar Therapy for Suspected Increased Intracranial Pressure

recommendations.statement: If hyperventilation is used for signs of active and imminent herniation, use capnography and target ETCO2 of 30– 35.
recommendations.context: Hyperventilation for active and imminent herniation.
recommendations.rationale: Hyperventilation can lower ICP, although its risks and benefits in this subset remain less clear.

recommendations.statement: Do not administer hyperosmolar therapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline before hospital arrival as prophylactic treatment for suspected elevated ICP, whether or not signs of cerebral herniation are present.
recommendations.context: Prophylactic treatment of suspected elevated ICP.
recommendations.rationale: Relevant prehospital studies failed to demonstrate improved outcomes with hyperosmolar fluids for this purpose.
recommendations.source_heading: Treatment: Hyperventilation and Hyperosmolar Therapy for Suspected Increased Intracranial Pressure

recommendations.statement: Do not regard prehospital TXA administration as generally or widely indicated to prevent suspected ICH or elevated ICP. Health care systems may make different decisions, and further evidence could support broader use.
recommendations.rationale: The cited studies do not establish an overall benefit for this use.

recommendations.statement: Establish an organized trauma care system in every region and comprehensively document the timing, assessment, and care provided for each encounter.
recommendations.context: Regional organization of prehospital trauma care.
recommendations.rationale: Organized trauma systems support coordinated care and timely access to appropriate resources.

recommendations.statement: EMS systems should establish specific protocols for deciding the destination of patients with suspected traumatic brain injury (TBI).

recommendations.statement: Prefer pediatric trauma centers or adult trauma centers with added qualifications to treat children over LevelI or II adult trauma centers without those pediatric qualifications for children with suspected TBI.
recommendations.rationale: The reviewed evidence supports care at trauma centers with pediatric capabilities.
recommendations.source_heading: Diagnosis: Decision-Making Within the EMS System: Dispatch and Destination, On-Scene, and Transportation

recommendations.statement: Transport patients with suspected moderate-severe TBI directly to a facility with immediately available computed tomography (CT) neuroimaging, prompt neurosurgical care, and capacity to monitor ICP and treat intracranial hypertension.
recommendations.rationale: These patients may need timely specialist assessment and definitive intervention.

recommendations.statement: Although direct transport to a trauma center is preferable for most patients, when it is not possible, initial stabilization at a non-trauma center followed by transfer within an established trauma system may occur.
recommendations.context: Alternative destination when direct trauma-center transport is not possible.
recommendations.rationale: The reviewed literature does not establish a definitive benefit of direct over indirect trauma-center transport for adults with TBI.

recommendations.statement: In metropolitan areas, transport pediatric patients with severe TBI directly to a pediatric trauma center when one is available.

recommendations.statement: Choose the mode of transport that minimizes the time until the patient with TBI receives needed definitive interventions.
recommendations.context: Selection of ground or air transport.
recommendations.rationale: Transport decisions must account for timely access to the interventions the patient needs.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: An estimated 69 million people sustain TBI worldwide each year. Incidence in low- and middle-income countries is three times that in high-income countries; reported fatality rates range from 5.2/100,000/year in France to 80.73/100,000/year in South Africa. TBI results from direct or indirect force that disrupts brain function and spans concussion through coma and death. Most injuries are mild, although prehospital distinction from more severe injury can be difficult. In the United States, TBI accounts for 2.87 million emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and deaths annually; approximately one-third involve children. After physical trauma, a GCS score <15, loss of consciousness, multisystem injury requiring an advanced airway, or a reported post-traumatic seizure raises concern for moderate-severe TBI. TBI markedly increases mortality after blunt trauma, and deaths from severe TBI often occur within the first few hours. Early care seeks to prevent secondary injury from cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemia, increased ICP, metabolic disturbance, hypoxia, and temperature instability. United States TBI fatality rates rise with increasing rurality, including for unintentional and assault-related injuries; the all-cause rate is 22% higher in rural than urban areas. Longer transport and reduced access to prehospital care may contribute. EMS professionals generally begin assessment and treatment at the scene and continue through hospital handoff, but personnel, equipment, training, and capabilities vary considerably across systems. A review of protocols in 32 U.S. states found practice variation and gaps in best practice. This evidence-based guideline addresses prehospital assessment and management of primary and secondary brain injury. Earlier Brain Trauma Foundation recommendations, first published in the 2000s, were initially graded “weak” because supporting evidence was limited. Subsequent evidence, including the Arizona Excellence in Prehospital Injury Care (EPIC) initiative, has linked guideline adherence in severe TBI with better outcomes. Figures 1 and 2 depict overall TBI fatality and the rural–urban disparity.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The workgroup developed an evidence-based update for prehospital TBI care in adults and children, organizing its questions around assessment, treatment, and decision-making.

document_sections.heading: Expert Workgroup and Topic Refinement
document_sections.content: Candidates came from participants in the Brain Trauma Foundation (BTF) 2nd Edition Guideline, relevant publications, and recommendations from academic, medical, and health organizations. Using PICOT, the group defined adult and pediatric topics and clinical questions. At least four participants initially worked on each topic and refined its scope and search terms. The final workgroup comprised 22 members who declared financial and intellectual conflicts. Table 1 outlines the assessment, treatment, and EMS decision-making topics covered.

document_sections.heading: Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria
document_sections.content: Eligible studies concerned human subjects with TBI, were in English, included 25 subjects, and used randomized controlled, cohort, casecontrol, case-series, database, or registry designs. Exclusions included interventions unrelated to the topic; outcomes unrelated to mortality, morbidity, or clinical outcomes; statistical methods unsuitable for the design, variables, or sample size; and case studies, editorials, comments, and letters.

document_sections.heading: Literature Search Strategy and Evidence Review
document_sections.content: The review was registered with PROSPERO and used methods from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality and National Academy of Medicine, with systematic-review and observational-meta-analysis reporting frameworks. A research librarian searched topic-specific literature from May of 2005 through November 2019 using Ovid MEDLINE and Cochrane Data Base, plus ClinicalTrials.gov for unpublished ongoing or completed trials. Workgroup suggestions and reference lists supplemented the searches. Records from 2005–2019 were deduplicated in Covidence. Two reviewers independently screened abstracts and full texts; a third resolved disagreements when needed. An additional PUBMED search for December 2019 through January 2021, using “prehospital” and “traumatic brain injury,” identified 124 abstracts, led to full-text review of 16 publications, and used four as related evidence for recommendations. Studies could inform multiple topics. Where publications shared data, reviewers retained the original or the more detailed or recent report with more patients. In total, 122 studies were evaluated. Two reviewers extracted study design, year, setting, location, size, eligibility, patient and intervention characteristics, and results; a third verified extraction. Population, intervention, and setting details informed applicability assessment.

document_sections.heading: Data Synthesis, Quality Assessment, and Classification of Evidence
document_sections.content: Prespecified, design-appropriate criteria assessed individual-study quality separately for assessment and treatment questions. The criteria drew on the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, National Health Service Center for Reviews and Dissemination, and Cochrane Collaboration. Evidence designated Class I, II, or III corresponded to low, medium, and high risk of bias. Two reviewers assessed quality independently, with third-reviewer adjudication to consensus. The full team met for a 2-day session and subsequent virtual discussions to agree on evidence classification and recommendation strength. Body-of-evidence assessment considered study limitations, consistency, directness, and precision. Overall grades were high, moderate, low, or insufficient: high indicated strong confidence in a stable effect estimate; moderate indicated some deficiencies and residual uncertainty; low indicated substantial deficiencies requiring more evidence; insufficient indicated absent or very limited evidence, or deficiencies that prevented a conclusion. Bias, inconsistent results, indirectness, and imprecision could lower quality. Contradictory findings from two or more Class I studies, or indirect evidence from Class I or II studies, could yield low overall quality.

document_sections.heading: Assessment: Oxygenation, Blood Pressure, and Ventilation
document_sections.content: This topic addresses prehospital recognition and monitoring of oxygenation, blood pressure, ventilation, and temperature after suspected TBI.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: After primary injury, hypoxia, hypoperfusion, and ischemia can produce secondary injury before hospital arrival. Hypotension impairs cerebral perfusion and outcomes; even brief hypoxia or hypotension is harmful, and their combination has a greater effect than either alone. Care aims to preserve cerebral perfusion while arranging rapid definitive treatment. Evidence suggests historical oxygen-saturation and blood-pressure treatment thresholds may be too low. Pending more conclusive evidence, clinicians should anticipate and prevent deterioration rather than wait for an established low reading; suspected TBI calls for continuous surveillance and prompt correction of hypoxia and hypotension.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Recommendations use strength and evidence quality based on the aggregate body of studies, assessed qualitatively or by meta-analysis. Following GRADE methods, “strong” and “weak” express confidence that benefits of adherence outweigh disadvantages. Strong recommendations derive from high-quality evidence with precise effect estimates; weak recommendations reflect uncertainty about the balance or size of effects. Indirect and related evidence, later publications, and workgroup consensus also informed decisions. A: Carefully monitor suspected TBI for hypoxemia (<90% arterial hemoglobin saturation), hypotension (<100mmHg SBP), hypertension (150mmHg SBP or higher), hyperventilation (end tidal CO2 less than 35), and abnormal temperature (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). a: Aim for pediatric SBP at the 75th and greater percentile for age (Strength of Recommendation: Weak): 28days and younger >70mmHg; 1–12months > 84mmHg; 1–5years >90mmHg; 6years and older > 100mmHg; Adults 110mmHg and above. b: In adults, aim for SBP 110mmHg or greater; lower values are associated with worse outcomes, although no firm cutoff is established and the optimum may be higher (Strength of Recommendation: Weak). B: Measure oxygen saturation continuously by pulse oximetry and give supplemental oxygen to keep it above 90% (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). a: Use pediatric sensors of appropriate size (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). b: Aim for saturation of 90% or greater after TBI; no firm cutoff is established, lower readings are associated with worse outcomes, and the optimum may be higher (Strength of Recommendation: Weak).
