C: Measure systolic and diastolic pressure by the most accurate available method every 5–10min or continuously if feasible (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). a: Use appropriately sized pediatric cuffs; where unavailable because of resource limitations, continuously follow documented mental status, peripheral pulse quality, and capillary refill as surrogates (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). b: Match cuffs to patient size (Strength of Recommendation: Strong): Infants 6x12cm; Children 9x18cm; Small adult 12x22cm; Adult 16x30cm; Large adult 16x36cm. D: In every patient with altered consciousness, assess ventilation by continuous capnography and maintain end tidal CO2 between 35 and 45mmHg (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). E: Measure temperature and seek euthermia of 98–99degrees Fahrenheit/36–37degrees Celsius (Strength of Recommendation: Weak). F: Outside resource-limited settings, trained prehospital personnel should routinely have appropriately sized adult and pediatric equipment for oxygenation, blood-pressure, and temperature measurement (Strength of Recommendation: Strong).

document_sections.heading: Evaluation of the Evidence: Quality, Applicability, and Summary
document_sections.content: Quality of Evidence: Moderate (one Class I, seven Class II; and nineteen Class III studies). Twenty-seven studies inform the topic; 11 carried forward from the 2nd Edition. Cohort studies related physiological measurements and interventions to mortality and function. Most retrospective reports used multisite databases, several prospective reports involved multiple centers, and studies came from the United States, Sweden, United Kingdom, Japan, Australia, Malaysia, and Italy. Eight enrolled only children younger than 18years; 11 combined children and adults. Most studies (21) examined hypotension. They associated prehospital hypotension with higher mortality and reduced survival to hospital and discharge. Whereas older work commonly defined hypotension as SBP <90mmHg, newer studies question a discrete threshold and associate increases from any baseline with better outcomes. Pediatric studies associated SBP more than the 75th percentile for age with the best outcomes; reviews also linked very high early SBP (160mmHg and higher) to higher mortality. Measuring and correcting oxygenation and preventing hypoxia were associated with improved outcomes. Two ClassIII studies found untreated isolated hypoxia was not significantly associated with death or disability, whereas two other Class III studies associated isolated hypoxia with morbidity or poor outcomes. Most studies found co-occurring hypoxia and hypotension more harmful than either alone. In one retrospective study of 299 children, approximately one-third lacked appropriate prehospital blood-pressure and oxygenation monitoring. One temperature study associated euthermia with better outcomes. Earlier guideline editions linked hypoxia and abnormal blood pressure strongly to poorer outcomes in moderate-to-severe adult and pediatric TBI; newer findings reinforce active identification and correction. An Italian air-transport study of 55 patients recorded saturation <90% in 55%. In a San Diego registry analysis of 3,420 patients with moderate-to-severe TBI, ED-arrival PO2<110 was associated with reduced survival (OR0.54, 95%CI0.42, 0.69 p<0.0001). A prospective cohort reported 37% mortality among patients with hypoxia (<92%). These findings support continuous or nearly continuous pulse oximetry. In a San Diego prehospital RSI study, each of 59 patients was matched to three nonintubated historical controls; SpO2<70% and a single desaturation <90% were associated with higher mortality (OR3.89, 95%CI1.12–13.52 and 3.86, 95%CI1.18–12.61, respectively). Continuous oximetry during intubation permits prompt correction. Traumatic Coma Data Bank data defined field hypotension as one SBP less than 90mmHg and hypoxemia as apnea, cyanosis, or saturation <90%; one hypotensive episode was associated with a two-fold mortality increase in matched cohorts. The observational EPIC analysis of 13,151 prehospital patients found higher pre-implementation odds of death with hypotension (OR2.49, 95%CI1.87–3.32) and hypoxia (OR3.00, 95%CI2.37–3.78); their combination was associated with 43.9% mortality and adjusted odds of death of 6.1 (95%CI4.20–8.86). EPIC also associated greater depth-duration exposure below 90mmHg with higher mortality, exceeding 50% after markedly prolonged hypotension. Across prehospital SBP 40mmHg to 119mmHg, EPIC associated each 10point increase with an 18.8% decrease in adjusted odds of death (adjusted OR, 0.812; 95%CI0.748–0.883), without a detectable inflection point. A Japan Trauma Data Bank analysis of 12,537 severe-TBI patients proposed defining hypotension as SBP <100mmHg below age 61years and <120mmHg at older ages; it identified 110mmHg as an optimal threshold, with adjusted admission-mortality odds of 1.58 (95%CI1.46–1.76, p< 0.001). Shibahashi et al. analyzed 34,175 patients in 2021 and significantly associated SBP < 110mmHg with in-hospital mortality. Elevated pressure can also be harmful. A registry review of 305,503 patients reported adjusted mortality odds of 1.33 at prehospital SBP 160–180mmHg (95%CI1.22–1.44, p<0.001) and 1.97 at 190–230mmHg (95%CI1.76–2.21, p< 0.001). A German registry analysis of 8,788 patients from 1993 to 2008 found mortality of 25.3% with hypertension >160mmHg versus 13.5% in normotensive patients (p<0.001), and reported an in-hospital mortality odds ratio of 1.9 (95%CI1.4–1.6). The discussion calls for monitoring at least every 5minutes to anticipate and address physiological insults. Pediatric evidence remains limited: among 299 children at a Level I center, pressure and oxygenation were recorded during part of early care in 31% and 34%, respectively, and 118 (39%) had documented hypotension. Failure to attempt hypotension treatment was associated with death odds of 3.4 and disability likelihood 3.7 times that of treated children; untreated hypoxia alone was not significantly associated with either outcome, but combined insults were associated with poorer outcomes. More hypotensive episodes were associated with longer hospitalization, pediatric intensive-care stays, and ventilation. In a United Kingdom study of 39 children admitted between 2002 and 2015, prehospital SBP <70mmHg was associated with higher mean ICP during the first 3days. A registry study of 10,473 children associated admission SBP <75th percentile with higher in-hospital mortality across age groups after isolated severe TBI. PEGASUS, conducted at five pediatric centers, defined hypotension as SBP less than 70+2 (age in years) and hypoxia as PaO2 <60mmHg or saturation <90%. Early hypotension occurred in 26% (60/234), with in-hospital mortality of 23.3% versus 8.6% (p= 0.01). Its authors associated treatment within 30minutes using intravenous fluids, blood products, or vasopressors with reduced in-hospital mortality (aRR0.46%; 95%CI0.24, 0.90); hospital-based observations may not readily generalize to prehospital care. Hypoxia occurred in 17% (41/236), and all affected patients received early treatment. This update incorporated 16 new studies and added adult and pediatric pressure targets, cuff sizes, ventilation monitoring, a weak temperature recommendation, and resource-related provisions. Proposed research addresses isolated versus sustained hypoxia, single versus sustained hypotension, optimal ETCO2 with and without intubation, and pediatric prehospital hypotension and hypoxia.

document_sections.heading: Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale and Other Assessment Scales
document_sections.content: This topic examines the use of GCS, P-GCS, and simpler neurological scores in prehospital assessment and prognosis.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: GCS and P-GCS are widely used to describe consciousness after TBI. Developed in 1974, GCS separately scores eye opening, motor response, and verbal response, enabling repeatable standardized neurological reporting. Its motor component conveys prognostic information close to that of the full score, although prehospital accuracy and inter-rater reliability have limitations. SMS and SVS were developed as simpler alternatives. Hypoxia and hypotension can impair responses and require immediate care, so airway, breathing, and circulation should be assessed and stabilized before GCS or P-GCS. Total prehospital scores help gauge injury severity and allocate trauma resources. Scores may differ between scene and ED because of improvement or deterioration after stabilization. Hypoglycemia and sedative or opioid overdose are reversible influences that should be identified and treated promptly. Table 2 contrasts GCS and the developmental modifications in P-GCS. The 1998 pediatric course supported assigning a full verbal score(5) for crying after stimulation in children under 2years; a prospective cohort found comparable accuracy of P-GCS for clinically important TBI in preverbal children below age 2years.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: A: Use standard adult GCS procedures in children over 2 years of age and P-GCS in preverbal children (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). B: Report GCS every 30minutes and after a mental-status change; document seizures, the post-ictal period, ingestions, overdose, and administered medications that may alter the score (Strength of Recommendation: Weak). C: Obtain the score through direct patient interaction, using verbal directions or a painful stimulus, such as nail-bed pressure or axillary pinch, when commands cannot be followed (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). D: Score after assessing airway, breathing, and circulation, establishing a clear airway, and completing necessary ventilatory or circulatory resuscitation (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). E: When feasible without delaying airway stabilization, score before sedatives or paralytics, or after their effects have resolved (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). F: Appropriately trained prehospital professionals should perform adult and pediatric scoring (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). G: Communicate the score and any changes to receiving facilities during communications and at arrival (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). H: Adult trauma systems organized to use SMS or the isolated GCS motor component may do so because these measures may have diagnostic and prognostic utility similar to total GCS (Strength of Recommendation: Weak).

document_sections.heading: Evaluation of the Evidence: Quality, Applicability, and Summary
document_sections.content: Quality of Evidence: Moderate (1 Class II study, 17 Class III studies, and 2 systematic reviews of high and low quality). Of 20 studies, 19 were new and one carried forward from the 2nd Edition; the set comprised two systematic reviews and 18 individual studies. They addressed severity recognition, mortality, intervention needs, scoring accuracy, and training. Most were retrospective registry analyses, principally from the United States, with studies also from the United Kingdom, Taiwan, Iran, Germany, and Israel. One enrolled only children younger than 18years and another mixed adults and children; applicability was moderate. Prehospital scores and changes by hospital arrival inform prognosis, management, and destination. Several studies found moderate inter- and intrarater reliability. Scores generally improved after field stabilization. ED GCS sometimes predicted function better than scene GCS, but findings differed between studies. RTS and TRISS also predicted outcomes. Retrospective designs and missing data limited interpretation. Winkler et al. observed higher ED than scene scores across outcome categories and found scene scores did not predict eventual outcome: mean GCS changed from 4.3 to 8.8 with favorable outcomes and from 4.4 to 5.7 with unfavorable outcomes. A European registry study restricted to brain AIS 3 or greater found higher median admission scores and higher admission-score AUC than scene-score AUC; motor scoring performed similarly to total GCS, but substantial missing scene data required imputation. Davis et al., studying RSI in patients with severe TBI and GCS 3 through 8, found very good agreement between paramedic and ED-physician scores derived from EMS reports, yet scene-score survival prediction had AUC0.63 and poor accuracy for ICU stay, ISS, and AIS. In another Davis et al. study of AIS3 or greater, field and arrival scores correlated strongly; mortality-prediction AUC was 0.84 at both times, with optimized cutoffs of 5 in the field and 6 at arrival. TRISS accurately predicted discharge survival in intubated and nonintubated patients. Najafiet al. assessed RTS, ISS, NEWS, SI, MSI, and TRISS in 185 patients for 24-hour mortality; prehospital NEWS and in-hospital RTS performed best in stepwise modeling. Combining GCS with pupillary size and reactivity generally improved prognostic accuracy, but markedly abnormal pupils with a poor GCS did not invariably predict adverse function and should not alone stop treatment. Among patients presenting with GCS 3, Sadaka et al. reported favorable 6-month GOS 4–5 in 14.5%, 14-day mortality of 66% versus CRASH-predicted 81%, and favorable GOS in 6.9% of those with bilateral fixed pupils. Favorable outcomes accompanied lower APACHE IV scores, fewer bilateral fixed pupils, and less ICP burden. Hoffman et al. reported mortality-prediction AUC 0.808 for GCS, AUC0.830 for GCS plus pupil size and reactivity, and AUC 0.827 for GCS plus reactivity; 8.0% with fixed dilated pupils reached GOS4 or better. Two age-stratified studies found more severe injury in older than younger patients at the same GCS, although retrospective design limits inference. Rau et al. compared elderly (65years) with non-elderly patients and found higher GCS among older patients within the same AIS category. Caterino et al. found thresholds of 14 at age 70years and 13 at age 16–70years produced similar sensitivity and specificity across groups. Across four observational samples, one meta-analysis, and one systematic review, total GCS generally predicted outcomes well; motor response was its strongest component, SMS often performed similarly, and no alternative was consistently superior. Proposed advantages in simplicity or reproducibility were not robustly evaluated. Thompson et al. reported GCS AUC of 0.70 for emergent intubation, 0.66 for clinically meaningful brain injury, 0.70 for neurosurgical intervention, and 0.82 for in-hospital mortality. SMS performed less accurately, but differed by at most 0.08 points and was considered similar by the authors. Caterino and Raubenolt reported mortality AUC 0.82 for SMS and AUC0.85 for GCS, with differences for other outcomes no greater than 6%; SMS and the isolated motor component had identical comparative findings. Haukoos et al. found total GCS AUC highest, with component and SMS results within 0.06 across outcomes; mortality AUC was 0.92 for GCS and 0.89 for SMS, without assessment of inter-rater agreement. Gill et al. found GCS most accurate across outcomes; the SMS mortality confidence interval (0.86 0.89) encompassed the GCS AUC estimate of 0.89, and interrater reliability could not be assessed. A Singh et al. meta-analysis of over 100,000 patients found pooled GCS AUC slightly above SMS AUC for four outcomes, with differences less than 0.04; heterogeneity and potential bias made clinical importance uncertain. Chou et al. likewise found slightly greater adverse-outcome accuracy for total GCS than its motor component; evidence that motor scores improve inter-rater agreement was low level, and training tools might help. Scene and ED scores generally agreed, with changing clinical state explaining some differences. In an Israeli blunt-trauma database study that excluded GCS scores over 123, Becker et al. found severe injury without TBI in 42% of hemodynamically unstable patients (SBP <90mmHg); incomplete TBI-severity characterization limited interpretation. Gang et al. developed a score combining GCS, hypotension, hypoxia, and age that correlated strongly with mortality in a Korean database, but external validation is needed because it arose in one trauma system.

document_sections.heading: Pediatrics
document_sections.content: A GCS of 12–15 reflects higher integrative function, which can be difficult to assess before neurological maturation. Expected verbal and motor behavior should therefore reflect developmental stage; standard GCS does not suit infants or preverbal children. The 1998 pediatric course supports full verbal score(5) for spontaneous cooing in preverbal children. In children aged 5–18years, Nesiama et al. found scene and arrival scores agreed strongly (Cohen’s kappa 0.69); mean scene scores were 0.43 points lower than ED means, without a median difference. Both predicted discharge function measured by GOS and Disability Rating Scale. In a German severe-TBI cohort that included 8.9% aged 15years, Emami et al. found lower pediatric than adult mortality overall and among patients with GCS 3 and bilateral fixed pupils (80.9% vs. 85% in that subgroup). Greater use of pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation might have contributed. In the combined cohort, absent motor response, bilateral fixed pupils, and dilation independently accompanied higher mortality; pediatric functional outcomes were better, and the authors suggested early aggressive care may benefit patients 15years of age. The update incorporated 18 new studies, strengthened recommendations, set a 30minutes reassessment interval, and added documentation of confounders and routine hospital communication. It weakly permits simplified scoring within suitable trauma systems. Research priorities include causes and prognostic effects of scene-to-ED score changes, effects of transmitting scores, effects of central-nervous-system depressants, reliability of simplified scoring, training interventions, examination findings relevant to triage, and improved documentation.

document_sections.heading: Assessment: Pupil Examination Introduction
document_sections.content: Pupil size, symmetry, and light reactivity inform immediate decisions and prognosis after TBI. Abnormal responses or asymmetry can accompany deterioration and poor neurological outcomes; pupillary reactivity combined with GCS helps predict 6-month mortality in moderate-to-severe TBI. Metabolic, medication-related, and toxic causes also warrant consideration. Serial assessment can detect change: anisocoria greater than 1mm may signal increased ICP or an enlarging lesion with possible transtentorial herniation, although practical benefit from infrared pupilometry has not been established. Bilateral examination assesses size, symmetry, and direct and consensual responses to light. Absent or asymmetric reflexes can indicate herniation or brainstem ischemia. Globe rupture, hyphema, medications or illicit drugs, prior surgery, lighting, malformations, genetic conditions, and ocular prostheses can affect interpretation.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: A: After resuscitation and stabilization, assess pupils before hospital arrival, document findings, and relay them to the receiving facility for diagnostic, treatment, and prognostic use (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). B: Examine and record orbital or ocular trauma; left–right differences, with clinically important diameter asymmetry defined as >1mm; unilateral or bilateral dilation; fixed and dilated pupils, defining fixation as <1mm response to bright light; and examination confounders (Strength of Recommendation: Strong).

document_sections.heading: Evaluation of the evidence: Quality, Applicability, and Summary
document_sections.content: Quality of Evidence: Moderate to Low (0Class I, 2ClassII, 10ClassIII). This topic included 13 studies, eight newly added and five retained from the 2nd Edition. They addressed field examination for diagnosis and prognosis and the implications of bilateral fixed dilated pupils for treatment. Despite predominantly Class III evidence, consistent findings and large datasets supported an overall moderate assessment in the discussion. One fair-quality study and five poor-quality studies, including four adult studies and one pediatric study, addressed field examination. In 121 patients with severe TBI, Sobuwa et al. found bilateral pupillary reactivity independently predicted good outcome, increasing its odds by 341%. Hoffman et al. analyzed 24,115 German registry cases and found reactivity plus the GCS motor component particularly predictive of mortality; equal, reactive, nondilated pupils before resuscitation accompanied the lowest mortality. McCabe and Donahue reported 100% mortality among eight children with bilateral fixed pupils on arrival within a 2000 study of 30 children with shaken baby syndrome. Among 62 patients with severe TBI and GCS 3, Sadaka et al. reported good 6-month outcomes in 7% despite bilateral fixed pupils. Studies totaling 185 patients with bilateral fixed dilated pupils reported mortality of 94% (87 of 93) retrospectively and 88% (81 of 92) prospectively. Approximately one in 10–20 field patients with this finding nevertheless had good functional outcomes, supporting continued early aggressive management. Transtentorial compression can produce anisocoria and reduced light response. Physiologic asymmetry of no more than 1mm with preserved reactivity occurs in up to 20% of people depending on lighting; a difference less than 1mm is considered normal. Among 310 healthy volunteers providing 2,432 paired measurements, asymmetry greater than 0.5mm appeared in less than 1% and was reportedly uncommon in TBI unless ICP exceeded 20mmHg. Chesnut et al. analyzed 608 severe-TBI cases: asymmetry had 30% positive predictive value for a mass lesion, with almost 80% of lesions contralateral to the pupil finding; anisocoria sensitivity was 40%, specificity 67%, and positive predictive value only 43% even with a difference greater than 3 mm. A single asymmetry measurement therefore neither reliably identifies nor localizes a mass lesion. In 672 patients aged 0–80+ years, Mamelak et al. ranked age, initial motor examination, then pupil response as outcome predictors. Brainstem ischemia, uncal herniation, direct brainstem injury, and marked ICP elevation may affect pupils; hypoxemia, hypotension, and hypothermia can also cause dilation or abnormal responses, making stabilization before examination important. Direct cranial nerveIII trauma may cause abnormalities without major intracranial injury, and asymmetric constriction can create apparent contralateral dilation. Pupillary findings are useful for immediate decisions and longer-term prognosis but do not specifically establish injury anatomy or severity. The update added eight studies, refined recommendations on confounder documentation and hospital communication, and identified research needs concerning device accuracy and repeated field examinations.

document_sections.heading: Treatment: Airway, Oxygenation, and Ventilation Introduction
document_sections.content: Prehospital airway care seeks to prevent hypoxia and identify patients likely to benefit from endotracheal intubation while avoiding peri-intubation hypoxia, hypotension, and hyperventilation. Hypoxemia strongly predicts outcomes after acute TBI. Relevant studies examine assessment, equipment, techniques, professional training and skill maintenance, recognition of esophageal placement, difficult or failed airways, medication adjuncts, oversight, monitoring, and quality improvement. The central question is when field intubation improves neurological outcomes or reduces mortality.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: A: Give continuous supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula or face mask to every patient with suspected severe TBI to reduce hypoxic secondary injury (Strength of Evidence: Strong). B: Use continuous oximetry to identify SpO2< 90% and immediately correct it through airway positioning and continuous supplemental oxygen (Strength of Evidence: Strong). C: If central cyanosis or oximetry-confirmed hypoxia persists despite increased oxygen flow and concentration, reassess saturation and respiratory effort after each sequential intervention: reposition the airway while considering cervical injury; provide positive-pressure bag-valve-mask ventilation with suitable adjuncts; and use a supraglottic airway or endotracheal intubation by a trained professional when needed (Strength of Evidence: Strong). D: Establish an airway by the most suitable available method when severe TBI accompanies inability to maintain adequate airway patency, or supplemental oxygen does not resolve hypoxemia (Strength of Evidence: Strong). E: Systems using intubation, including RSI, should verify tracheal placement by bilateral breath sounds and ETCO2 detection and/or capnography; continuously monitor oxygenation and ETCO2 and frequently check pressure in intubated patients (Strength of Evidence: Strong). F: When positive-pressure support is needed, use approximately 10breaths per minute and target ETCO2 35–45mmHg; avoid ETCO2 <35mmHg. Pressure-controlled bags, rate timers, ETCO2 monitoring, and ventilators should support appropriate rates and avoidance of both under- and overventilation (Strength of Evidence: Strong).

document_sections.heading: Evaluation of the Evidence: Quality, Applicability, and Summary
document_sections.content: Quality of Evidence: Moderate (3ClassI, 5ClassII, 12ClassIII). The update included 20 studies: 14 newly added and two retained directly from the 2nd Edition, plus two systematic reviews. Of 27 studies originally included in that edition, 10 were covered by the reviews rather than current evidence tables; another twelve were descriptive or addressed surrogate outcomes. Questions concerned indications and methods for intubation, paralytics, RSI sedatives, ventilation targets, and pediatric–adult differences. New evidence emphasizes prompt correction of hypoxia and hypocapnia while uncertainty remains about who benefits from field intubation. The guideline defines hypoxemia as saturation <90% and/or central cyanosis. Its discussion calls for continuous highflow oxygen even when a patient with suspected TBI is normally oxygenated, ideally recording saturation every 5minutes and maintaining >90%. Persistent hypoxia prompts repositioning, bag-valve-mask ventilation with suitable adjuncts, consideration of supraglottic devices, then intubation by an experienced advanced-life-support professional if oxygenation or ventilation remains inadequate. Severe TBI with GCS <9 warrants immediate consideration of an advanced airway. In a German registry review of 21,242 patients, field-intubated patients with GCS <9 had a smaller difference between observed and predicted mortality than nonintubated patients. Intubation evidence is conflicting. An earlier retrospective study of 981 patients intubated in prehospital or ED settings associated emergency intubation with death (odds ratio 14.3; 95%CI9.4–21.9), without establishing a prehospital-specific effect. A Class III Sydney study of 310 suspected-TBI patients with GCS <14 from 2007 to 2013 found no survival-to-discharge improvement with field versus ED intubation (73% vs. 70%, p= 0.69). In a United States matched registry analysis of 8,139 field-intubated patients, the intubated group had longer scene intervals (median 9 vs. 8minutes p< 0.001), longer transport intervals (median 26 vs. 19minutes p< 0.001), lower ED GCS (3.7 vs. 3.9, p= 0.026), and higher hospital mortality (31.4 vs. 27.5%, p<0.001). A review of 17 studies through 2007 did not support a benefit from field intubation and mechanical ventilation. Another review searched through 2015 and included 30 studies, with 24 in its systematic review and six in meta-analysis. It reported higher mortality odds after intubation by less-experienced professionals (OR2.33, 95%CI1.61–3.38, p< 0.001) than after intubation by more-experienced professionals (OR0.75, 95%CI0.52 to 1.08, p=0.13). Its authors judged evidence of benefit from trained-professional intubation insufficient, although overall-outcome trends favored it. The single randomized trial in these reviews, by Bernard et al. in 2010, reported favorable-outcome odds of 1.6 after prehospital versus in-hospital intubation. A United States multicenter ClassI study reported favorable outcomes in 882 patients and associated field intubation of blunt moderate-to-severe TBI with GCS 4 to 12 with favorable neurological outcomes of 57.3% versus 46.0% without field intubation (p= 0.003), and mortality of 13.8% versus 19.5% (p=0.03). Adjusting for index GCS, mortality odds were 47% lower (OR0.53, 95%CI0.36–0.78). However, 80% of intubated patients traveled by air, and the neurological association was not significant after transport mode adjustment. Among intubated patients, adjusted death odds were higher with ground than air transport (OR2.10, 95%CI1.40–3.15), although ground outcomes trended better than no intubation. The investigators associated field intubation during air transport with favorable outcomes and lower mortality, and did not associate field intubation with increased morbidity or mortality across transport methods or injury severities.

document_sections.heading: Treatment: Airway, Oxygenation, and Ventilation
document_sections.content: Evidence reviewed in this update emphasizes training and continued proficiency in prehospital intubation, including recognition of esophageal placement, management of difficult or failed airways, and use of RSI to improve first-pass success. Studies discussed in the 2nd Edition Guideline reported intubation success of approximately 85%, compared with 39% in historical controls with GCS <9 and suspected TBI, after changes to training and equipment that included RSI. They also reported mortality of 41% in the RSI group versus 30% among patients who were not intubated (OR1.6; 95%CI1.1–2.3), and good neurologic outcomes of 37% versus 49% (OR1.6; 95%CI1.1–2.3). Those studies did not assess indications for intubation; 32% of prospectively enrolled intubated patients did not have TBI. An Australian study likewise found greater intubation success with RSI, but no significant improvement in mortality or ICU length of stay. Earlier research associated hyperventilation and hypocapnia with worse TBI outcomes, supporting continuous ETCO2 assessment by waveform capnography. Shortly after TBI, cerebral blood flow may fall by as much as two thirds of normal in approximately half of patients; hyperventilation can reduce it further and potentially cause ischemia. Inadvertent hyperventilation during transport is frequent and is associated with higher mortality. In a U.S. study, severe hyperventilation on hospital arrival (pCO2<25) occurred in 15% of patients receiving prehospital RSI and 8% of controls who were not intubated. Avoiding hyperventilation is therefore central to prehospital resuscitation. The Arizona EPIC implementation study used an intention-to-treat, controlled before-and-after design across EMS systems for moderate to severe TBI between 2007 to 2015. Its protocol applied continuous high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask to maintain oxygen saturation greater than or equal to 90%, advised pre-oxygenation, and escalated inadequate oxygenation or ventilation to bag-valve-mask ventilation and then intubation if that failed to correct hypoxia. For adults greater than 15years of age, it used 10 breaths per minute and a two-finger bag technique; continuous ETCO2 monitoring targeted 40mmHg within 35–45mmHg. Of 21,852 eligible patients, 15,228 were in the preimplementation phase, 6,624 in the post-implementation phase, and 4,014 required intubation. Implementation was not associated with a significant improvement in overall survival to discharge. Survival to discharge improved in severe-injury subgroups: Regional Severity Score-Head 3–4, aOR2.03; 95%CI1.52–2.72, p< 0.001; Injury Severity Score 16–24, aOR1.61; 95%CI1.07–2.48; p= 0.02. After implementation, SpO2 of 100% and reversal of hypoxemia became more likely, hyperventilation or hypocapnia among intubated patients became less frequent, and intubation decreased while BVM-only management increased, despite greater brain and overall injury severity. This update added 14 new studies to a body of evidence of moderate quality and strengthened recommendations on airway care, oxygenation, ventilation, continuous hypoxia monitoring, stepwise airway management, and avoidance of hyperventilation. Proposed research includes effects of training on airway proficiency, outcomes with different sedatives during prehospital RSI, and variation and best practices among airway-management systems.

document_sections.heading: Treatment: Fluid Resuscitation Introduction
document_sections.content: Fluid needs may differ between hypotensive polytrauma and isolated TBI, requiring resuscitation to be adapted to the circumstances. Prehospital fluids aim to prevent hypovolemia, hypotension, and secondary brain injury. Adult and pediatric definitions of hypotension differ. Existing evidence suggests historical blood-pressure treatment thresholds may be too low; pending more conclusive evidence, such as a randomized study, care should emphasize avoiding the threshold region rather than waiting for an established low reading. Fluid treatment principally seeks to increase cardiac preload and preserve cardiac output and cerebral oxygen delivery without hemodilution or additional blood loss. Injury mechanism, including blunt or penetrating trauma, can affect fluid selection and volume. Options include isotonic or hypertonic crystalloids and colloids, including blood or blood substitutes.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Intravenous fluids should be given before hospital arrival to treat hypotension and/or keep its duration as short as possible (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). Prehospital hypotension should be treated with isotonic fluids and/or blood products when indicated and available (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). Hypertonic fluid resuscitation may be used when GCS <8 and increased ICP is suspected in the prehospital setting (Strength of Recommendation: Weak).

document_sections.heading: Evaluation of the Evidence: Quality, Applicability, and Summary
document_sections.content: Quality of Evidence: Moderate (0ClassI studies, 10Class II studies, 3Class III studies). The update considered 13 studies: six new and seven retained from the 2nd Edition Guideline, including two systematic reviews and five individual studies. Comparisons of resuscitation fluids were limited by few new studies and small trials; reported outcome differences between fluids were limited and uncertain despite possible biological and biomarker differences. Hemorrhage reduces cardiac preload and, when compensation fails, tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery. Blood-product resuscitation restores preload and supports cardiovascular function and oxygen transport. In TBI, reduced cerebral perfusion can extend neurologic injury or worsen outcomes, and hypotension has been shown to cause secondary brain injury. In a prospective series involving 6,908 adults and 1906 children less than 15years of age at 41 centers, Luerssen et al. associated hypotension with significantly higher mortality in every age group, with a greater adverse effect in children. When hypotension occurs, blood pressure and oxygen delivery should be restored promptly without provoking hemodilution or further bleeding. Because blood or fluid loss is almost always its underlying cause in these patients, intravascular volume replacement is the most effective means of restoring blood pressure. By contrast, early blood-pressure restoration worsened outcomes in penetrating torso trauma; the relevance of those findings to TBI is unknown. Crystalloid has been the most frequently used fluid to support preload, cardiac output, and peripheral oxygenation; a common prehospital approach is a bolus of 1 to 2 liters. In children, clinical evidence of poor perfusion warrants fluids even if a blood-pressure reading is adequate. Hyperoncotic or hypertonic fluids and hemoglobin substitutes permit potentially smaller, faster infusions, but their TBI outcome benefits have been inconsistent: favorable results in earlier, lower-quality studies were not reproduced in larger, methodologically stronger trials. Four randomized, double-blind trials by Vassar et al. in the early 1990s examined combinations of isotonic fluids, hypertonic saline, and dextran. They described prehospital hypertonic saline as safe and potentially beneficial, without additional benefit from dextran. Another hypertonic-versus-normal-saline trial found no outcome difference. In a comparison of hypertonic saline with Ringer’s lactate involving 166 patients, 32% with severe TBI, logistic regression favored survival with hypertonic saline. In a study of 258 patients, 10% with severe TBI, survival among those with GCS less than 8 or severe anatomic cerebral injury exceeded TRISS predictions with hypertonic saline whether or not dextran was added. A multicenter 1993 trial of 194 patients, 74% with severe TBI, reported better survival with hypertonic saline than Ringer’s lactate in patients described as having GCS scores 8. In Wade et al.’s review, survival to discharge was 38% with hypertonic saline and 27% with standard therapy (p=0.08); logistic regression comparing hypertonic with isotonic fluids yielded odds ratios of 1.92 for 24-hour survival and 2.12 for survival to discharge (p= 0.048). Cooper et al.’s 2004 randomized, double-blind prehospital trial enrolled 229 patients with severe TBI and hypotension. It included multitrauma but excluded comorbid conditions, peripheral edema, and close proximity to hospital; after an initial 250mL bolus, standard resuscitation continued in the field and hospital. Outcomes did not differ between fluid groups. Tan et al.’s 2011 review included nine randomized trials and one cohort study and concluded that hypertonic fluids and dextran did not improve functional outcomes. In Junger et al.’s 2013 nonprehospital comparison of 250ml normal saline, hypertonic saline, and hypertonic saline plus dextran, outcomes did not differ. Blanchard et al.’s 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis found no outcome advantage for hypertonic over isotonic saline, but included trauma beyond TBI. Bergmans et al.’s 2020 review and meta-analysis found insufficient evidence that any particular prehospital fluid improved outcomes. These studies did not identify harm from hypertonic solutions, leaving systems to weigh risks and benefits when selecting fluids. Six new studies improved the assessed quality of evidence and strength of recommendations without substantially changing their content. Further research is sought on prehospital hypertonic saline and TBI outcomes, cognitive recovery separately from blood-pressure resuscitation, and the effectiveness of hypertonic solutions as plasma-volume expanders.

document_sections.heading: Treatment: Hyperventilation and Hyperosmolar Therapy for Suspected Increased Intracranial Pressure
document_sections.content: Early detection and treatment of increased ICP matter for TBI outcomes. Traditional indicators are Cushing’s triad—hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing—GCS <9, posturing or lateralizing signs, worsening neurologic function, and one or two fixed, dilated pupils. These signs may lack adequate sensitivity and may delay definitive care. Increasing respiratory rate enhances CO2 elimination; lower CO2 constricts cerebral microvessels, reduces intracranial blood volume, and lowers ICP. This rationale previously led to preventive or prophylactic hyperventilation when raised ICP was suspected. Prospective observational studies from the early 2000s subsequently reported higher mortality and fewer good neurologic outcomes after prehospital RSI than among patients not intubated. The RSI groups also had more severe hypocarbia on hospital arrival, suggesting hyperventilation contributed to excess mortality; hypocapnia-induced vasoconstriction could cause microvascular ischemia and accumulation of lactate and glutamate. Prehospital and hospital evidence now links routine hyperventilation to worse TBI outcomes. ETCO2 monitoring is therefore important; monitored patients have less severe hyperventilation, and capnography-guided ventilator adjustments during transport significantly reduce hypocapnia at trauma-center arrival. Intracranial bleeding can produce mass effect and increased ICP. Prehospital tranexamic acid (TXA) has been proposed to limit hemorrhage expansion, but a large NIH-funded placebo-controlled multicenter trial comparing two prehospital TXA dosing regimens in moderate to severe TBI found no differences in 28-day mortality, intracranial-bleeding progression, or 6-month GOS-E. TXA does not directly treat elevated ICP and lies outside this treatment topic.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: In children and adults with TBI who lack signs of active cerebral herniation, prehospital hyperventilation should be avoided (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). Signs listed for active herniation are Cushing’s triad—hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing—GCS <9, posturing or lateralizing findings, progressive neurologic deterioration, and unilateral or bilateral fixed, dilated pupils. Ventilation should aim for eucapnia, ETCO2 of 35–40, avoid hypocapnia, and be monitored with capnography (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). If hyperventilation is used for active and imminent herniation, capnography should guide an ETCO2 target of 30– 35 (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). Mannitol and hypertonic saline should not be given before hospital arrival to prevent suspected elevated ICP, whether or not cerebral-herniation signs are present (Strength of Recommendation: Weak). Prehospital TXA is not generally or widely indicated to prevent suspected ICH or raised ICP; health systems may differ in their decisions, and further evidence could support broader use (Strength of Recommendation: Strong).

document_sections.heading: Evaluation of the Evidence: Quality, Applicability, and Summary
document_sections.content: Quality of Evidence: Moderate (1ClassI, 2ClassII, 7ClassxcIII). This topic examined 10 studies, comprising four new studies and six retained from the 2nd Edition Guideline. Hyperventilation can lower ICP through cerebral vasoconstriction but also decreases cerebral blood flow. ClassII hospital evidence associated prolonged hyperventilation with worse outcomes at 3 and 6months and equivalent outcomes at one year. Two new studies and one retained study evaluated prehospital hyperventilation in severe TBI; several older studies instead collected descriptive hospital data. Expanding intracranial hemorrhage and cerebral edema are common causes of raised ICP. Hyperosmolar agents create an osmolar gradient that draws extracellular fluid into the circulation and improves viscosity, but no identified high-quality study directly examined their acute prehospital use for raised ICP.

document_sections.heading: Hyperventilation
document_sections.content: Davis et al. associated prehospital hyperventilation in severe TBI with unfavorable outcomes and lower PaCO2 at ED arrival with poorer outcomes. Dumont et al. described hyperventilation in patients without actual herniation and found increased mortality risk with both hyperventilation and hypoventilation. Caulfield et al. linked hyperventilation negatively with mortality and GOS-measured neurologic function. Spaite et al. reported better survival to hospital after implementing Brain Trauma Foundation guidance that included avoidance of excessive and inadequate ventilation. Unintended prehospital hyperventilation may be frequent; capnography is essential for ETCO2 assessment but does not itself guarantee its prevention. Although most evidence does not show benefit from early hyperventilation, its balance of risks and benefits is less certain when there is objective evidence of active, imminent herniation. Possible field signs include dilated or unreactive pupils, asymmetry, posturing, and worsening neurologic status—a GCS decrease of more than two points from the patient’s prior best score—but their predictive values are moderate to low. The discussion describes maintaining PaCO2 at 35–45mmHg, avoiding inadvertent hyperventilation during transport, and using PaCO2 monitoring to confirm ventilation. It calls for correcting hypoxia by raising inspired oxygen tension rather than respiratory rate. It also says transient hyperventilation to a PaO2 level of 30–35mmHg may be considered for clinical signs of active herniation only when surgical decompression or other interventions will not be rapidly available; this PaO2 wording differs from the recommendation’s ETCO2 target.

document_sections.heading: Hyperosmolar agents
document_sections.content: Mannitol and hypertonic saline can temporarily lower ICP, but a high-quality prehospital trial has not demonstrated an outcome effect for mannitol. Schwartz et al.’s comparison with pentobarbital did not establish pentobarbital’s superiority and reported better outcomes and preservation of cerebral perfusion pressure in the mannitol group. Hypertonic saline is a low-volume resuscitation option and brain-directed hyperosmolar treatment. Animal and human studies found that bolus hypertonic saline reduces ICP in controlled operating-room or ICU settings with ICP monitoring, but evidence that acute administration improves morbidity or mortality is minimal. Intravenous normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is isotonic and theoretically produces little osmolar movement. Hypertonic solutions raise extracellular tonicity; supplied concentrations include 3%, 7.2%, 7.5%, 10%, and 23.4%. No definitive evidence identifies an optimal concentration or bolus-versus-continuous delivery for ICP reduction, and differing study protocols impede comparisons. Unlike mannitol, no study reported hypertonic saline’s effect on clinical herniation signs such as pupillary changes or posturing. Hospital hypertonic-saline treatment often targets serum sodium around 155–160mEq/L, hypothesized to stabilize ICP and lessen treatment intensity; that target is not feasible before hospital arrival. A ClassII study found no neurologic-outcome advantage for prehospital hypertonic saline over normal saline as a resuscitation fluid. A ClassIII comparison of 1.6% saline with lactated Ringer’s solution found no outcome difference, although baseline differences and other factors limited interpretation. One Class II and one ClassIII study failed to show outcome improvement with prehospital hyperosmolar fluids. Available literature consequently does not support prophylactic prehospital ICP reduction with mannitol or hypertonic saline.

document_sections.heading: Tranexamic Acid
document_sections.content: TXA has been investigated before hospital arrival to prevent intracranial bleeding, rather than as a direct raised-ICP treatment. CRASH-3 suggested benefit in mild to moderate TBI, but not severe TBI. The randomized, double-blind, multicenter phase II Prehospital TXA for TBI trial at 20 U.S. and Canadian trauma centers found no statistically significant benefit. The prospective multicenter observational BRAIN-PROTECT study involved 680 TXA-treated patients, found no overall outcome benefit, and reported increased mortality in the treated group. On this evidence, benefit of prehospital TXA in severe TBI remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Pediatrics: Additional Considerations
document_sections.content: A pediatric severe-TBI guideline states that hyperventilation’s effect on long-term pediatric outcomes has not been studied; its recommendations drew indirectly on adult evidence. This update describes 10 new studies as improving a body of evidence of moderate quality and strengthening recommendations. Its revisions discuss TXA without recommending prehospital use, caution against hyperventilation, and recommend capnography. Proposed research addresses accuracy of field indicators of increased ICP, comparative performance of ventilation-control devices, effects of transient hyperventilation for suspected imminent herniation, effects of prehospital hyperosmolar treatment in that situation, indications for hypertonic resuscitation in children, and TXA’s possible role.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis: Decision-Making Within the EMS System: Dispatch and Destination, On-Scene, and Transportation
document_sections.content: Prehospital decisions must balance need for trauma-center resources with transport mode and time. Personnel estimate injury severity rapidly with limited field diagnostics and may need to choose between a nearby hospital and a more distant higher-level center; ground-versus-air decisions may also affect TBI morbidity and mortality. A U.S. study associated care for severely injured adults at a LevelI-II trauma center with a 25% lower adjusted overall risk of death. The American College of Surgeons Field Triage Decision Scheme, updated with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, uses four steps to identify severe injury in general trauma patients, but strict application has limitations. Under-triage—failure to treat a severely injured patient at a Level I or II facility—has been associated with greater mortality. Over-triage—bypassing nearer hospitals when higher-level services are unnecessary—can burden distant patients and families, increase patient and crew safety risks, and remove ambulances from community service for longer. An organized trauma system helps match patients to needed care. Direct trauma-center transport is preferable for most patients; when impossible, initial stabilization at a non-trauma center followed by transfer within an established system may occur (Strength of Recommendation: Weak). In metropolitan areas, children with severe TBI should go directly to a pediatric trauma center when available (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). Transport mode should minimize time until needed definitive intervention (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). Quality of Evidence: Moderate (1ClassI study, 8ClassII studies, 30ClassIII studies). The update considered 39 prospective and retrospective cohort studies—28 new and 11 from the 2nd Edition Guideline—using sources ranging from large national or state registries to single centers. Evidence addresses five areas: regional trauma organization, direct versus indirect transfer, trauma-center level, transport mode, and time to treatment. Findings were inconsistent within each area, potentially reflecting differences in setting, regional standards, and practice.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: Every region should maintain an organized trauma-care system and comprehensively record encounter timing, assessments, and care (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). EMS should establish explicit destination protocols for suspected TBI (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). For children with suspected TBI, pediatric trauma centers or adult centers additionally qualified to treat children should be preferred over LevelI or II adult centers lacking those pediatric qualifications (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). Suspected moderate-severe TBI should be transported directly to a facility with immediately accessible CT neuroimaging, prompt neurosurgical care, and capacity to monitor ICP and treat intracranial hypertension (Strength of Recommendation: Strong). Recognition and management by prehospital personnel can influence outcomes; decisions by EMS telecommunicators, first responders, and receiving hospitals occur sequentially, as depicted in Figure3.

document_sections.heading: Regionalization of Trauma Care
document_sections.content: Organized regional care has shown outcome benefits in ST-elevation myocardial infarction, stroke, and trauma, and is fundamental to an effective trauma system. Timely arrival at a neurotrauma-capable facility is associated with less TBI morbidity and mortality. After regional trauma-system implementation, one U.S. study reported preventable deaths falling from 20% to 1% (p<0.005) in patients without TBI and from 5% to 0.7% (p<0.10) in patients with TBI. Another U.S. retrospective study reported a mortality odds ratio of 0.80 after implementation. Hunt et al.’s 1995 study found a nonsignificant fall in overall severe-TBI mortality but significant reductions in time to emergency decompression and mortality among patients needing it. After a rural hospital met LevelII verification criteria, survival among all patients with calculated survival probability of 25% rose from 13% to 30%; among TBI patients it rose from 15.4% to 32%. In a New York State registry study spanning 3-year, patients with head injury who met one or more physiologic field-triage criteria had significantly lower mortality when taken to regional trauma centers instead of nontrauma centers (OR0.67; 95%CI0.53–0.85). No effect was identified for other injuries, although the study was not powered to detect those differences. A new ClassII study identified 3,496 severe-TBI patients in one trauma system: 1,359 before and 2,137 after regionalization. In-hospital mortality fell significantly from 19% to 14% (p<0.0001), and six-month mortality from 24% to 20% (p=0.004). Functional independence measures did not change significantly. Its authors interpreted increased survival as neither worsening nor improving neurologic outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Direct versus Indirect Transport to a Trauma Center
document_sections.content: Field priorities are stabilizing immediate threats and preventing secondary injury while rapidly selecting an appropriate destination. Coordinated prehospital care, triage, and trauma-center admission may improve general-trauma outcomes, but advantages of early stabilization and later transfer must be balanced against over-triage. Available evidence has not established a definitive advantage for direct trauma-center transport over initial nontrauma-center care followed by transfer in adults with TBI. Using a 2012 national ED sample, Fakhry et al. found almost 20% of all severe-TBI ED visits resulted in admission outside a LevelI or II center, accounting for 45% of severe-TBI ED visits presenting to those centers. Patients with isolated TBI taken directly to LevelI or II centers were more often admitted (89% vs. 45%) and had significantly higher predicted mortality (11.3% vs. 6.8%). At lower-level centers, death probability did not differ significantly between admitted severe-TBI patients and those transferred to LevelI or II centers. Kuimi et al. reviewed 22,749 major-trauma records, with 89% transported directly to trauma centers; among TBI patients, direct transport did not significantly change hospital mortality or length of stay. They suggested that appropriate initial triage within the established system could explain the finding. Gale et al.’s rural TBI study over 6-year found that 44% received initial referral-center assessment and stabilization. Patients taken directly to LevelI centers were significantly younger and had higher ISS and lower GCS; adjusted mortality related significantly to age and ISS, but not distance or transfer time. Pickering et al.’s systematic review of 19 studies published from 1988 through 2012 found no significant overall outcome difference with direct transport. Of three adjusted head-trauma studies, one favored direct specialist transport and two favored transfer, without significant findings; pooled mortality showed no significant difference and high heterogeneity, and an unadjusted analysis of 10 studies also found no significant difference. Nishijima et al. studied 350 older patients (age > 54), 73% directly transported to LevelI or II centers, and found no functional-outcome difference. In the prospective European CENTER-TBI study, involving 22 European countries and published by Sewalt et al. in 2021, 195 of 1,347 patients with moderate or severe TBI arrived through secondary referral. Case-mix adjustment found no functional-outcome or survival effect of transport route. Its observational design, missing data, and possible omission of deaths before transfer limited interpretation; the study underscored early blood-pressure and oxygenation management. One Class I cluster-randomized study found no 30-day mortality difference between direct neurosurgical-center transport and initial nonacute-hospital transport followed by transfer. Ambulance stations were assigned to transport strategies, but enrollment reached only 293 patients over 12months against a target of 700, and only 24% had CT-confirmed TBI. Substantial over-triage, low enrollment, and limited protocol adherence constrained generalizability. Two ClassIII studies suggested potential direct-transport benefit. Prabhakaran et al. studied transfers over 2years to a LevelI center—64.7% direct and 35.3% secondary—and found no overall mortality difference, but, for GCS <9, secondary transfer entailed significantly longer waits for neurosurgery and higher mortality. In Johnson et al.’s prospective, nonrandomized pediatric comparison, mortality was 4.7% with indirect versus 1.9% with direct transport to a pediatric LevelI center. Trauma scores differed significantly at baseline; the authors proposed that delayed-transfer deterioration could itself account for the difference and suggested immediate pediatric-center transport might improve survival in that metropolitan setting.

document_sections.heading: Level of Trauma Center (Type of Treatment)
document_sections.content: American College of Surgeons trauma-center levels reflect resources as well as education and research commitments. LevelI and LevelII centers both have TBI-care resources. Evidence does not definitively favor direct LevelI over LevelII transport, although some mixed-quality studies suggest a LevelI advantage. Among rural-center patients later transferred, McConnell et al. reported a 10% absolute reduction in 30-day post-discharge mortality after transfer to LevelI rather than LevelII centers. A National Trauma Data Bank retrospective study found significantly higher mortality after initial LevelII transport in TBI (adjusted odds ratio 1.57; 95%CI1.41–1.75) and significantly fewer complications among patients treated at LevelI centers. Other studies suggested little or no LevelI advantage. Cornwell et al. observed significantly shorter times to operating room and ICU after one center gained Level1 designation; an apparent severe-TBI hospital-mortality improvement was not statistically significant. Lombardo et al. found no significant survival difference for isolated TBI in neurosurgical versus trauma ICU care, suggesting generalized trauma care at a LevelII center might be adequate. Alkhoury and Courtney reported non-inferior mortality and complications for isolated TBI taken to LevelII versus LevelI centers. For adolescents, evidence does not definitively prefer pediatric to adult trauma centers, but pediatric capability is supported for children with TBI. Gross et al.’s 2017 study of patients aged 15 to 17years found no significant adult-versus-pediatric center outcome difference, including after accounting for LevelI versus LevelII status. Potoka et al. found better survival in pediatric centers for severe TBI among patients aged 0 through 16years; children requiring neurosurgery had lower survival at adult LevelII centers than at other trauma-center types. Bardes et al. compared isolated TBI in children aged <14years and found significantly higher mortality at adult than pediatric centers (OR1.55, p= 0.01), without a significant difference between pediatric and mixed adult/pediatric centers. Their interpretation emphasized access to pediatric subspecialists.

document_sections.heading: Mode of Transport
document_sections.content: Transport decisions include ground versus air and, for ambulances, emergency lights and sirens. They depend on urgency and whether advanced on-scene skills are needed. Evidence suggests possible helicopter benefit in severe TBI, although added air-service clinical capabilities may explain some of it. Bekelis et al. compared helicopter with ambulance transport to LevelI or LevelII centers. Before propensity matching, helicopter patients had lower mean GCS, higher mean ISS, and higher overall mortality (12% vs. 7.8%); after matching, helicopter transport was associated with significantly better survival at LevelI (OR1.88, 95%CI1.74–2.03) and Level II centers (OR1.73, 95%CI1.55–1.94). In the same databank, Aiolfi et al. found helicopter transport independently associated with survival despite higher injury scores (OR0.55, 95%CI0.47– 0.67). Sun et al. found greater inhospital survival for helicopter-transported skiers and snowboarders with isolated TBI (OR8.58, 95%CI1.09–67.64). Baxt and Moody reported a 9% mortality reduction with helicopter transport, but helicopter crews included a physician and nurse whereas ground crews had a paramedic. Davis et al. retrospectively analyzed 10,314 patients with head AIS scores of 3 or more and reported better adjusted survival odds with helicopter transport (1.90; 95% confidence interval 1.6 to 2.25), particularly with more severe injury indicated by lower GCS. An Italian comparison found longer scene times but shorter time to intervention and significantly lower mortality with helicopter transport (21% vs. 25%, p<0.05). Both modes carried nurses and physicians; helicopter crews had advanced-airway capability, intubated more often, and administered more intravenous fluid. Conversely, Bulger et al.’s retrospective analysis of prospective trial data found no significant adjusted difference in 24-hour or 28-day survival between air and ground transport of adults with severe TBI without hemorrhagic shock. Air patients had longer scene times, greater injury burden, and higher predicted mortality. Di Bartolomeo et al. also found no significant outcome difference between ambulance nursing care and helicopter physician care. An older registry study found no air-versus-ground outcome difference. In de Jongh et al.’s 2012 matched study, a nonsignificant tendency toward higher helicopter mortality had OR1.3, 95%CI0.6–2.7; after controlling for scene interval, the comparison was still nonsignificant (OR0.8, 95%CI0.4–2.0). Pediatric air-transport evidence is limited. Missios and Bekelis associated helicopter transport with greater adjusted survival at LevelI (OR1.77, 95%CI1.25–2.52) and LevelII centers (OR2.56, 95%CI1.28–5.11), although air patients were more severely injured and had higher unadjusted mortality. Heschl et al. reported favorable neurologic outcomes in 66% versus 17% (p=0.06) for helicopter versus ground transport among children with TBI and major trauma. The small sample and intubation of every air patient but no ground patient complicate interpretation. Given uncertain pediatric benefit, helicopter use might be excessive in some situations. Elswick et al.’s algorithm, derived from pediatric referrals to one Level I center rather than injury-scene transports, favored reserving air transport for GCS 3–8, CT-demonstrated mass effect or herniation, cerebral edema, epidural hematoma, or open depressed skull fracture. Time to specialist intervention remains relevant to every mode decision.

document_sections.heading: Time to Treatment
document_sections.content: Whether longer prehospital intervals worsen TBI outcomes remains unclear. General training promotes rapid transport so surgery can occur within the first hour after injury when needed, and clinical experience identifies patients helped substantially by rapid care; reviewed prehospital evidence nevertheless does not establish a definitive interval–outcome association. Severe-TBI acute subdural hematoma was associated with 90% mortality when evaluated more than 4 hours after injury versus 30% with earlier evaluation. Hunt et al. reported a 70% mortality decrease when subdural hematoma was evaluated less than 2hours after injury. Wilberger et al. found no statistically significant overall mortality difference by time to surgery, although surgery within 4hours was associated with a 10% absolute mortality reduction compared with treatment greater than 4hours; that study did not assess benefits from other hospital interventions. Di Bartolomeo et al. found no outcome difference despite an almost 60-minute difference in time to receiving-facility arrival. Lokkeberg and Grimes found time to definitive care was not a significant adjusted outcome predictor in severe blunt TBI. A 2011 study found scene time greater than 60minutes was not associated with poor outcome, though intubated patients had significantly longer scene intervals. Fuller et al. found neither scene time nor overall EMS interval significantly associated with vital-sign deterioration during transport. Although 25% had vital-sign changes, adjusted analyses did not relate their magnitude to EMS interval. A 2015 registry analysis found no significant association between EMS interval and 30-day inpatient mortality for adults admitted to neurologic specialty centers after significant TBI, including analyses adjusted through propensity matching. Newgard et al. compared out-of-hospital intervals less than 60minutes and greater than 60minutes. Patients with GCS less than 9 and transport times greater than 60minutes had higher ISS, more airway procedures, and more air transport, but no significant difference in 6-month neurologic outcomes or 28-day mortality. Meizoso et al. associated field interventions with lower mortality in severe trauma without significantly longer scene times. Collectively, these findings suggest the care delivered on scene may matter more than scene duration alone. Two newer studies suggested possible benefit from faster specialty-center transport. Among traumatic-subdural-hemorrhage patients, Tien et al. associated each additional scene minute with higher mortality (OR 1.03; 95%CI1.005–1.05), but examined a small single-center cohort with 40% mortality. Dinh et al. reported a scene-time mortality hazard ratio of 1.002 per additional minute after adjusting for GCS (95%CI1.001– 1.004); after additional confounder adjustment, arrival within 1hour versus later showed no significant difference. This topic added 28 studies and improved evidence quality and recommendation strength without changing recommendation content. Proposed studies address dispatch identification and decisions, caller instructions, effects of field assessment, treatment and transport decisions, comparisons between organized and nonorganized trauma systems across professional skill levels and injury severities, transport time under special circumstances, minimum destination resources for severe TBI, and optimal destination for mild to moderate TBI.

document_sections.heading: Guideline Update and Conclusions and Summary of Future Directions
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that an extensive evidence base supports better outcomes with organized, scientifically informed prehospital TBI care. Field professionals must recognize possible brain injury rapidly, provide life-supporting interventions, use airway, breathing, circulation, and other physiologic measures to guide timely treatment, and plan transport while considering their own safety. Figure4 presents a prehospital assessment and management algorithm for suspected moderate to severe TBI. The guideline addresses important pediatric and geriatric differences but did not assess evidence on sex, geographic region, race or ethnicity, insurance, socioeconomic position, other medical conditions, and additional demographic or medical factors. The authors identify these gaps and topic-specific future research questions as priorities and suggest that high-quality controlled studies incorporating implementation plans have the greatest potential to affect care.

document_sections.heading: Algorithm
document_sections.content: For evidence assessment, individual studies are classified as “good,” “fair,” or “poor.” A “good” study has low risk of bias and results considered valid, supported by clear population, setting, intervention, and comparator descriptions; valid allocation or observational-group identification; limited and documented dropout; appropriate confounding control; and suitable outcome measurement. “Fair” denotes some possible bias without a flaw likely to create major bias. Missing information may impede assessment, and validity varies across this broad category. “Poor” denotes major design, analysis, reporting, missing-data, or intervention-delivery problems that can invalidate findings; results may reflect methodological defects rather than true intervention differences and receive less weight when evidence conflicts. Two review-team members assessed each study’s quality, with review by one to three topic-leading clinical investigators; disagreements were settled by consensus.

document_sections.heading: Data Synthesis
document_sections.content: Evidence tables record included-study characteristics, outcomes, and quality ratings, with condensed results presented in the article and detailed abstractions supplied to clinical investigators. Decisions about whether meta-analysis is meaningful consider study quality and differences in design, population, interventions, and outcomes. Key questions examine comparative effectiveness and harms across patient demographics, comorbidities, and treatment characteristics. Study information is summarized qualitatively, with descriptive interpretation available for clinical-investigator review.

document_sections.heading: Grading the Quality of the Body of Evidence
document_sections.content: For each key question and outcome, one researcher initially assesses evidence strength after identification and searching conclude, using Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality methods; the investigator panel and review team then examine the grades. Considered domains are study limitations, consistency, directness, and precision. The overall body of evidence receives “High,” “Moderate,” “Low,” or “Insufficient.” “High” reflects strong confidence that the effect estimate approximates the true effect, few deficiencies, and stable conclusions. “Moderate” reflects moderate confidence, some deficiencies, and findings likely to remain stable despite residual doubt. “Low” reflects limited confidence because of major or multiple deficiencies and a need for more evidence. “Insufficient” reflects absent or very limited evidence, inability or lack of confidence to estimate an effect, or deficiencies that prevent a conclusion.

document_sections.heading: Assessing Applicability
document_sections.content: Applicability concerns whether evidence can answer the intended questions in other populations and care settings. Variation among studies or unusual study attributes may restrict generalization, and assessment of applicability is not standardized. The review considers patient demographics, underlying condition or disability, comorbidities, geographic location, and practice context. Potential applicability concerns are identified during abstraction and quality assessment, then synthesized for the evidence body supporting each question and its recommendations.
